articles.title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to bar watchdog after confronting Sunday Times journalist
articles.summary:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his…

blocks.text: Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of a tirade at a journalist shortly after the comedian had been found guilty of rape.
Ian Winter KC confronted the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”
Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done”, to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”
“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened on Thursday afternoon outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court, with a group of journalists watching.
In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.

He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.
“I have made such a report.”

The incident at court happened moments after Brand had been found guilty by a jury of rape and three counts of sexual assault, at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.
Brand had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.

In an interview on Times Radio after the exchange, Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times, defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way. There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.

“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.

blocks.caption: A jury of eight men and four women found Russell Brand guilty of rape. Photograph: James Veysey/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.

“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury, a system that we support massively at the Sunday Times, and we have actually campaigned to protect, who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”
During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by Urwin and others had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for him to have a fair trial.
The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.

In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had also accused the journalists who first exposed Brand as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.
But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.
Brand, 51, was convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan in 2009 as well as sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009.
He is in custody and due to be sentenced on Monday.

articles.title: Federal judge temporarily halts building work on Trump’s triumphal arch
articles.summary:
US judge issues 14-day block on construction on DC monument after it was approved by planning commission

A federal judge in the early hours of Friday blocked any construction work from…

blocks.text: A federal judge in the early hours of Friday blocked any construction work from beginning on Donald Trump’s towering triumphal arch for 14 days, a major setback for one of the president’s most prominent projects in his vision to remake the nation’s capital.

The temporary restraining order was issued by US district judge Tanya Chutkan in a Washington DC court that has regularly proved to be a thorn in the US president’s side, such as in previous cases involving election subversion and the January 6 insurrection by Trump supporters.

The new ruling followed a series of steps taken on Thursday by the government, including the final approval of the 250ft-high (76 meter) arch by the National Capital Planning Commission in an 8-4 vote after a nine-hour hearing where dozens of witnesses opposed the construction.

The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. Those projects could soon face greater scrutiny after the Democrats gained control of Congress.

The administration had said the work on the arch could begin as soon as the approval and the interior department issued a final decision authorizing construction and the proper notification was published by the National Park Service.

In issuing the delay, Chutkan granted the request of the latest plaintiffs in lawsuits challenging the arch. Chutkan also consolidated lawsuits from the District of Columbia and Virginia with a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
It’s unclear how much the project will cost, or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100m.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump holds up a model for his proposed arch back in October 2025.   Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The vote by the planning commission on Thursday came after nine and a half hours and scores of people opposing it. The vote by the commission broke along federal and local lines. Those in favor work for the administration or are connected to the president, who was pushing for the immediate construction. Opponents represented the city of Washington.

The remote, call-in hearing – which crashed repeatedly in the first few hours and was accompanied by a nearly universally negative comment section – drew witnesses who gave impassioned comments opposing an arch that they said would destroy the solemnity of the nearby Arlington national cemetery, where hundreds of thousands of fallen service members and military veterans are buried.

“In my view, the disruption that the arch will cause to the unobstructed sight line, a symbol of national unity, will disrespect the memory of our veterans,” said Michael Lemmon, a Vietnam war veteran, former ambassador and lead plaintiff in the lawsuit against the arch, in a court filing in February 2026, when the suit was first filed.

“I hope to be interred in Arlington Cemetery alongside my fallen comrades when I pass away. The thought of being interred in the shadow of what I believe to be a personal vanity project is profoundly disturbing to me.”
The panel’s Trump-appointed chair launched the meeting with a gushing appraisal of the towering monument and lauded Trump for wanting to build it.
“President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it’s important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments,” said Mark Paoletta, the commission’s chair.

As Trump has often remarked, “the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London,” said Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget.

Commissioner Paul Ingrassia, a lawyer for the General Services Administration, said the arch was “not about politics. It’s about remembrance. It’s about celebrating our history. It’s about commemorating veterans. And it’s really something that’s a noble tribute to our nation and something that we can all rally behind.”

But DC city council member Phil Mendelson, who also serves on the planning panel, said the project had not received required approval from Congress, nor had Congress appropriated any money for it. The plan submitted to the commission does not include a reference to military use cited by Trump and other administration officials, Mendelson said.
“We cannot approve final site and building plans until we have the final site and building plans,” he said.
Representative Jared Huffman, a California Democrat who is set to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, called the project ill-advised and illegal.

“This arch would dishonor America,” Huffman told the commission. He called the proposed arch “a tribute to Donald Trump,” not veterans, as Trump administration officials claim. The monument is similar to those built for emperors or kings, Huffman said, adding that Trump was using veterans as a pretext to build a memorial to himself.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the difference between flame-based cremation and pet aquamation?
articles.summary: After the dead bodies of 29 cats and dogs were found carelessly dumped in parts of Bulacan when they were supposed to be cremated, a lot of fur parents began to fear that the ashes given to them by…

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 10:01pm

After the dead bodies of 29 cats and dogs were found carelessly dumped in parts of Bulacan when they were supposed to be cremated, a lot of fur parents began to fear that the ashes given to them by pet crematoriums were actually their pets.

In a report from GMA News Feed, the incident became viral online, making pet owners doubt if the ashes they have were actually their beloved animal companions. Some said that the color of the ashes they had was grey; others said that theirs were white.
So why do these colors differ?
There are different ways to process the remains of a pet. The flame-based cremation is often what comes to mind when one thinks of cremation.

According to the Cremation Association of North America, this process uses fires and extreme heat in a cremator to turn the remains into bone fragments. After it goes through the machine, the bones are processed and crushed finely. This is what the pet owners receive.
This is the common form of cremation being used in many funeral homes and crematories.
Other than flame-based cremation, however, there is also a form of cremation that uses water and chemicals. This is aquamation, or alkaline hydrolysis, where the decomposition phase is quickened.

In aquamation, the body of the pet is placed in a stainless-steel vessel with an alkaline solution. The machine uses heat and pressure to slowly melt the soft parts of the body until only the bones are left.
The bones are then dried and crushed into powder.
According to the American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA), aquamation leaves behind bones that are dried. This is why it is often whiter compared to ashes from a flame-based cremation.
U.S. based non-profit organization Environmental Literacy Council said that the colors of pet ashes may differ based on their diet, health conditions, and medication.
Following the Bulacan incident, Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) said that there are different ways to check the validity of the cremation services that fur parents are getting.

“It's sad that we have to ask the consumers themselves to be the ones to look out when there should be a regulatory function… On how they can check if the crematorium is legitimate, many of the legit crematoriums provide a step-by-step documentation of their pets' cremation,” PAWS Executive Director Anna Cabrera said in a mix of English and Filipino.

“I've seen pet parents show me that there is a timestamped video from the time that they took the animal, all the way to the cleaning of the body, sa pagpasok doon sa cremation machine, hanggang sa paglabas and kung paano nilagay sa urn, and it's given to them. And I think this should be the standard,” she added.
Cabrera advised fur parents that if they have doubts about the ashes that they are holding, they can bring it to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).
NBI Director Melvin Matibag said that they can do the forensic analysis to check.

“They can bring the ash to NBI, and they will do the forensic analysis, just to give them the assurance that it's really at least a cremated dog…But they're only going to be able to determine if it's the cremated remains of a dog, or a cat, or if it's wood, or if it's ashes, cement,” Cabrera said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Anti-fire ant eradication activist convicted after using legal arguments ‘similar to sovereign citizens’
articles.summary:
Legal expert compares Trevor Hold’s failed defence to ‘tried and tested argument’ used by sovereign citizen movement

  • Get our

blocks.text: The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.

Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.
He was convicted last month of two counts of obstruction for attempting to prevent fire ant treatment at his property, in what is believed to be a Queensland first.

His organisation and others held a series of well attended meetings last year across south-east Queensland to advise residents on what the group called their legal rights to refuse or prevent access to their properties to the program.
Under Queensland’s Biosecurity Act, landholders must permit program officers to access their property to treat fire ants, which are a declared priority pest.
But the organisations advised landholders to use a provision in the act allowing them to obstruct an officer if they had a “reasonable excuse” to refuse access, a provision in the Biosecurity Act.

On 16 April at about 9.20am, Hold prevented officers from entering his property in Adare in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane. The property was in the treatment zone and due for its annual treatment.

The eradication program had informed Hold in advance that it would treat his property that day. A small group of supporters gathered to film and yell at them while they did so, according to court documents.
The scene was later described as “an increasingly rowdy and crowded and dynamic situation” in the Ipswich magistrates court, which heard Hold’s charges last month.

He was arrested by Queensland police after about 40 minutes for obstructing them by not allowing a gate to be opened. He was then un-arrested. Despite being warned again, he was again arrested after another interaction with program officers.
Hold made three arguments to the magistrate, Leanne Scoines, in his defence.
He argued that he was intimidated by the police and the program officers and “withdrew his consent for their attendance”, describing himself as “frazzled”.
“It was put to Mr Hold that he was not frazzled, and that he had said on three occasions, as heard in the body-worn camera footage, that ‘this is the Trevor Hold show’,” Scoines said.
Through his lawyer, solicitor Beatrice Ludwig, Hold argued that the police had failed to take into account his “reasonable excuse” and were therefore acting outside their powers.

Hold based part of his argument on emails he sent to the Department of Primary Industries in December 2024 and January 2025, notices the magistrate described as “unilateral”, “quasi-legal documents … seeking tacit approval by non-response”. The magistrate found they were of no legal effect.
Finally, he challenged the validity of the program, arguing that the prosecution had not proven it was properly authorised under the Biosecurity Act, Scoines said.

All three arguments were dismissed and the magistrate found that the officers were entitled to proceed on the basis that the DPI officers were exercising powers conferred on them by the Biosecurity Act.
“I am not satisfied that Mr Hold was a credible or liable witness on the critical issues in dispute,” she said.
A police prosecutor told the court “In my respectful submission it was clear he was actually enjoying this incident”.
Hold has appealed against the judgment to the district court.
On his website, Hold advertises fundraising efforts for his defence, and also a mooted class action lawsuit against the program.
Hold would not comment on the case.

Southern Cross University professor David Heilpern compared some of the arguments used by Hold to sovereign citizen cases he used to judge as a magistrate in the NSW Northern Rivers region, particularly his claim that he hadn’t consented to fire ant treatment.

“That is a tried and tested argument in terms of many of those who are on the fringe of or deep into the sovereign citizen movement; that you have a right to remove consent from the operations of various laws,” Heilpern said.
“Whether you consent or don’t consent is completely immaterial under the biosecurity legislation.”

articles.title: The Victorian Liberals’ campaign bus was supposed to be a reset. Instead it became the symbol of a rough week
articles.summary:
Crashing into a shop awning ended the first outing of the Jess Express – but the opposition’s electoral momentum will be harder to stop

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business.
The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.

A day earlier, journalists had been left waiting for an hour as Wilson announced a $100m investment in medical research to an enthusiastic room of researchers at the Burnet Institute. But when it came to questions she stayed for just four minutes and 39 seconds – answering a single question from each of the nine journalists present before cutting the press conference short.
The pack had been keen to press Wilson on Labor’s claim that the Coalition’s election policies would cost $6.35bn more than they had disclosed.

The treasurer, Colin Brooks, had earlier spent 20 minutes taking journalists through a glossy booklet Labor titled “Jess Wilson’s Dodgy Costings”, which detailed 30 Coalition promises it claimed had not been costed and dozens it said the opposition had underquoted.

It was an interesting stunt given Labor has its own cost blowouts and financial problems – including net debt that is forecast to reach $199bn within four years. But they are not the only ones questioning how the Coalition plans to deliver a surplus by 2032 while making $8bn worth of election promises, offering tax cuts and vowing not to cut frontline services.
The Liberals have made much of their credentials as better economic managers than Labor and Wilson, as shadow treasurer, should have been prepared to stay and defend her own numbers.
The moment played into Brooks’s suggestion earlier in the day that the Liberals “don’t want to be subject to the scrutiny of having journalists … asking questions during the day”.
“They’re thinking they’re going to coast home to this election result, and that’s treating the Victorian people with contempt,” he said.
A similar thing happened last week, when Wilson’s team cancelled a press conference amid confusion over the Coalition’s plan to “pause and review” the multibillion-dollar Suburban Rail Loop project.

Then there is the debate brouhaha. Both News24 and Nine had requested a debate involving Wilson, the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, and the One Nation leader, Warren Pickering – given the latter is now commanding about 20% of primary votes in most polls.

Wilson has refused, instead insisting on a traditional one-on-one format with Labor, arguing that only the two major parties could form government. Carrollwants Pickering to be included, seemingly keen to keep alive the idea of a Liberal-One Nation coalition despite polling suggesting the Liberal-National Coalition should be able to win government in its own right.
Last week, News24 seemed to resolve the impasse by also inviting the Greens leader, Ellen Sandell.

But no agreement has been reached on Nine’s proposal. Wilson issued a statement on Thursday saying she had agreed to debate Carroll next week. This time Labor refused, claiming Nine has offered Pickering the opportunity to appear in a separate 10-minute segment during the same broadcast.
The Liberals reset on Friday, unveiling the “Jess Express” campaign bus.

Wilson was joined by her team and recruits from Canberra – including her close friend and federal Liberal senator James Paterson, and Kane Silom, who has taken leave from his role as communications director for the federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, to work on the Victorian campaign.
She chatted with journalists on the bus before it arrived at a Bentleigh cafe, where she made coffees and served brunch before a press conference, this time clocking in at more than 20 minutes.
Pressed again on her party’s costings, she said voters would have to wait until after early voting begins to see them.
“We cannot release our costings until the government has released its pre-election budget update,” Wilson said.

She batted off questions about the Liberals’ latest election commitment – to sell $1.3bn worth of government-owned land. Labor says this is more “dodgy costings” as it includes land earmarked for first home buyers, and a plot where radioactive cow carcasses were buried that would cost millions to clean up.
“Those costs have been factored in as part of the independent costings by the Parliamentary Budget Office,” Wilson said.
Then it was back on the bus and to the Centre Road shops – one of which became the victim of the Jess Express.
But perhaps there’s a glimmer of hope. Despite the damage, the store owner wasn’t too fussed, provided his awning is repaired.
Nor was it enough for him to rule out voting Liberal – he said he was still undecided.
It will take a little more to stop the Coalition momentum at this stage of the campaign.

items: Benita Kolovos is Guardian Australia’s Victorian state correspondent

articles.title: Oxford, Bethnal Green and the Guardian: surprising British backstory of senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed
articles.summary: In a Guardian article in 2010, the Oxford Rhodes scholar said UK democracy had the ‘upper hand’ over the US

blocks.text: In the tense final hours before his dramatic election as senator for Michigan in this week’s midterms, Abdul El-Sayed had a heated encounter with a British TV journalist that rapidly went viral.

As James Matthews, of Sky News, tried to ask him a question, El-Sayed bit back. “Why would I care to have a conversation with you?” he demanded of Matthews, placing both hands on the reporter’s shoulders in a gesture of emphasis.
“You know how many votes I want to get in the UK? Zero. I am never running for office in the UK. So I actually do not care what you think or the questions you ask.”

The clip has been viewed more than 13m times on X. But the pugnacious senator-elect has not always been so dismissive of British politics and voters. Guardian readers with longer memories may recall a young Rhodes scholar who in May 2010 wrote an article for this newspaper that declared – somewhat boldly for a future US senator – that “UK democracy has the upper hand on the US”.

blocks.caption: El-Sayed’s heated encounter with James Matthews of Sky News has been vewed 13m times on social media. Photograph: Sky News/Twitter X

blocks.text: El-Sayed was then a 25-year-old doctoral student at Oxford University and had just attended a Labour party hustings in Bethnal Green and Bow, east London, to choose a parliamentary candidate. That meeting, he wrote, had persuaded him that the UK’s electoral system was, in some respects, superior to that of the US, leaving him “envious” of the British way of doing things.

“As an American, born, bred, and taught in school that American democracy was the greatest in the world, I was initially sceptical of this foreign brand,” he wrote. “But what I experienced that evening was a ceremony in communal self-determination that I have yet to see in any federal American electoral institution.”

El-Sayed’s election in Michigan was one of the standout headlines of Tuesday’s poll after facing a barrage of racism and Islamophobia during the campaign. Donald Trump mocked his name, called him a “jihadist lunatic” and said the Senate would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. He was also denounced at the last minute by Haley Stevens, the Democrat congresswoman he had narrowly defeated for the nomination. She sensationally endorsed his Republican rival.

blocks.caption: El-Sayed campaigning in Royal Oak, Michigan. He faced a barrage of racism and Islamophobia, including from Donald Trump. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: El-Sayed cut a dash, too, in his campaign appearances, choosing to dress in a uniform of tight black T-shirts to show off a physique described by the BBC’s North America editor, Sarah Smith, as “jacked”.

It’s all a long way from Bethnal Green where, El-Sayed noted in his Guardian article, the smaller size of British constituencies compared with US electoral districts meant minority groups could more easily make their voices heard.

The larger number of parties competing for seats, too, meant elections became “a community exercise in cohesiveness and solidarity, antithetical to the American electoral climate”. And El-Sayed praised the fact that voters were focused on local concerns rather than being distracted by electing a head of state.
after newsletter promotion

“As an American observer, I thought I knew a thing or two about how a democratic debate is supposed to run …” he wrote. “While there are, undoubtedly, some excellent qualities in American democracy, my first hustings in Bethnal Green and Bow left me just a tad envious – what are the odds they’ll allow an American cast his vote on 6 May?”

They didn’t – and nor did El-Sayed’s British sojourn last. The future senator returned to the US in 2011 after completing his doctorate in public health (and captaining the Oxford lacrosse team against Cambridge, a match in which he got a yellow card).

In the the last of his pieces for the Guardian in January 2011, El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants to the US, challenged Barack Obama over his response to the Arab spring, writing: “When I helped elect you into office as the 44th president of the United States of America, I believed I was doing a service by my country”, and challenging him to support the “freedom fighters” who had risen up against Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak.

After his election on Tuesday, El-Sayed had a message for Trump. In an oft-repeated quip from the campaign trail, he said: “Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name. So after JD [Vance] swears me in in January, you can just go on and call me senator.”

articles.title: Czech arms makers set sights on space defense in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven arms boom
articles.summary: Czech arms makers have thrived on demand linked to the war in Ukraine. But to sustain their growth, they need to look beyond ammunition and toward new technologies — and even space.

image.caption: Russia's war in Ukraine has driven major growth across the Czech defense industry as a whole. Pictured here: a new facility for filling artillery ammunition at ZVS Holding, which is part of the Czech CSG groupImage: Dalibor Gluck/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Czech arms maker Czechoslovak Group (CSG) announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.
This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.
From 90s startup to major European player

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.

blocks.caption: When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG became the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe. Pictured here: CSG chairman and owner Michal StrnadImage: Jan Lopatka/REUTERS

blocks.text: It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.
The impact of the war in Ukraine
The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.
In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.
By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.
Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

blocks.caption: While drones play a major role in the war in Ukraine, both sides continue to attack each other with artillery fire. Czech defense contractors have responded by expanding production of military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bulletsImage: Jose Colon/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.
Historical link
"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.
Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.
At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
Export dependence
However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

blocks.caption: The populist ruling coalition under Prime Minister Andrej Babis (pictured here) is divided on the issue of support for UkraineImage: Beata Zawrzel/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.
As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike, German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."
What the future holds

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

blocks.caption: The US has repeatedly said that it expects its European allies in NATO to increase defense spending. Pictured here: US President Donald Trump speaking at the NATO leaders' summit in Ankara in JulyImage: Stoyan Nenov/REUTERS

blocks.text: The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."
Space mission
CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.

blocks.caption: Most Czech defense companies are already more technologically advanced and diversified than they were when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022Image: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.
Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.
"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

articles.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health
articles.summary: Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’

blocks.text: TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.

The Chinese-owned short-video platform, which has 189 million users in the EU, was found to have failed to prevent users from being served up repetitive content on themes such as body image or isolation, which can lead to anxiety, sadness, worsen existing eating disorders or mental health problems.

Officials said their investigation focused on legal content, where a single video might not be problematic, but the cumulative effect of watching scores of them on one theme could damage users’ mental health.

TikTok’s safeguards to mitigate the risks of “rabbit-hole effects” – where users are served narrow and repetitive content to keep them engaged – were found to be ineffective. For example, officials said, if a user checked a “not interested” button on a video about eating patterns, the algorithm would still offer them similar content on diet and body image. Similarly, refreshing a feed only provided a brief respite from a stream of content on one topic, it found.

“Every time a user scrolls or likes a video on TikTok, the algorithm serves more of the same leading users down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from,” the European Commission’s lead official on tech policy, Henna Virkkunen, said. “TikTok needs to step up its efforts to protect users’ wellbeing, including those of minors.”
TikTok has been contacted for comment.
The investigation strikes at TikTok’s business model, which is built on keeping users scrolling as long as possible.
EU officials want TikTok to change the design of its ForYou feed, to give users greater control over the content they see.

“We are addressing a business model,” a commission official told reporters, saying that a business model focused mainly on engagement “can potentially create a risk” especially for minors and vulnerable adults.

The findings are part of a broader investigation launched in February 2024 under the Digital Services Act, which obliges large internet companies to take action to prevent a wide range of harms, from disinformation to damage to mental health.

The commission has already found the company violated EU rules over its “addictive design” for features such as infinite scroll. The company said at the time: “The commission’s preliminary findings present a categorically false and entirely meritless depiction of our platform” and that it would challenge the findings.
A complaint about lack of transparency over who paid for TikTok’s advertising was resolved when the company made binding commitments to change its policies last December.
TikTok, which now has a chance to examine the investigation file and mount a defence, could agree to change its recommender system to avoid a fine.
If EU officials uphold the finding, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global worldwide turnover.

articles.title: China’s rocket launch moved to Monday
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard said that China’s Long March 12 rocket launch, initially scheduled on Friday, was moved to Monday, Nov. 9. In an advisory, the Coast Guard District…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Coast Guard said that China’s Long March 12 rocket launch, initially scheduled on Friday, was moved to Monday, Nov. 9.
In an advisory, the Coast Guard District Palawan (CGDP) advised mariners to take note on the new launch date of China’s rocket between 4:17 a.m. and 4:47 a.m. (Philippine standard time) on Monday.

It warned that rocket debris discarded during lift off are expected to fall within identified maritime drop zones 25 nautical miles (nm) away from Puerto Princesa City, Palawan and 19 nm away from Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park.

The identified drop zone is located within Philippine archipelagic waters. The CGDP warned that the debris’ potential impact may pose a threat to vessels transiting or operating within the affected areas.
It added that the rocket debris is not projected to plummet over the country’s landmass or inhabited areas.

“All concerned mariners and maritime stakeholders are strongly advised to exercise heightened vigilance, avoid navigating within the identified drop zone during the specified period, and monitor official announcements and navigational warnings for further updates,” it said in the advisory.

Based on the Philippine Space Agency’s memorandum, the initial launch was originally set on Friday, between 5:10 a.m. and 5:39 a.m. (PhST) from the Hainan International Commercial Launch Center in Wenchang, Hainan, China. /mr

articles.title: US job growth exceeds expectations in October despite economic uncertainty
articles.summary:
‘Low-hire, low-fire’ labor market shows sluggish growth but few layoffs, with an interest rate hike expected in December

The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of…

blocks.text: The US added 165,000 jobs to the economy in October, a sign of resilience in the labor market amid ongoing war in the Middle East and inflation, according to new data released on Friday.

Economists had said the labor market has been stuck in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, in which job growth is sluggish but layoffs also remain low, but October’s data surpassed economist expectations. The unemployment rate went down slightly to 4.1%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

Average hourly earnings increased at an annual rate of 3.1%, slightly higher than last month. Inflation over the last few months has largely outpaced the growth in wages – what often leads people to feel they are spending even more to buy essentials. In September, the annualized inflation rate was 3.7%.
Initial figures for August and September were also revised up by a total of 84,000 jobs. Job growth was seen in healthcare, transportation, warehousing and manufacturing.

Other data released earlier this week showed employment has been steady. Layoffs in September fell to their lowest level in a year and a half, according to the bureau, while outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas tracked just under 44,000 layoffs in October – a 71% decrease compared with last October.

The new data comes after a seismic midterm election that solidified Democrats’ control of Congress for the next two years. Multiple polls had shown Americans were most frustrated about the state of the economy, especially higher gas and grocery prices.

“Americans delivered a clear verdict in the midterm elections that the current economy is squeezing people financially and making it hard to get by, let alone get ahead,” said Heather Long, chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, in a statement before Friday’s report. “The labor market is a good example of why people are frustrated.”

But it’s unclear when Americans will get relief. Gas prices are on average $1 a gallon higher than they were a year ago because of the war in Iran. The price of diesel, which is used throughout the supply chain to power large vehicles, is 60% higher compared with prewar levels.

In times of stubborn inflation, the US Federal Reserve usually intervenes by raising interest rates, which slows price increases. In September, the Fed hiked interest rates for the first time since 2023, bringing them up to a range of 3.75%-4%, citing inflation. Though officials kept rates steady at their last meeting in October, held the week before the election, economists are expecting one more rate hikes at the next central bank meeting in December.

Meanwhile, markets over the last week have been shaken as investors appeared worried about AI spending. After reaching correction territory, when an index drops 10% below its most recent peak, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index briefly made a recovery on Wednesday before diving back into correction territory on Thursday.

articles.title: Canadian economy lost 4,700 jobs in October as unemployment rate ticked up to 6.7%
articles.summary: The loss of a few thousand jobs last month follows big back-to-back job losses in August and September, when the Canadian economy shed more than 100,000 roles cumulatively over two months.

image.caption: Applicants at the CNE’s job fair wait in line at the Enercare Centre in Toronto on July 30, 2025. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·Breaking
The loss of a few thousand jobs last month follows big back-to-back job losses in August and September, when the Canadian economy shed more than 100,000 roles cumulatively over two months.
Economists polled ahead of data release expected economy would add 13,600 jobs
Canada's unemployment rate rose to 6.7 per cent in October as the country shed 4,700 jobs, according to figures from Statistics Canada.

Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions in October, marking the first decline in the segment since February. On the flip side, the number of public employees — which had been in decline for four months in a row — rose by 50,000.
Statistics Canada says more young workers were looking for a job in October, too. Unemployment among people aged 15 to 24 rose by 0.7 percentage points to 13.7 per cent.
Unemployment among the core aged workforce — those 25 to 54 years old — held steady.
Economists polled by Reuters ahead of the release expected a gain of 13,600 jobs for October and for the unemployment rate to remain unchanged.

articles.title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe
articles.summary:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues

A fresh wave of bomb threats has disrupted air traffic across

blocks.text: A fresh wave of bomb threats has disrupted air traffic across Europe but the affected planes landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.

The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Czechia, France, Italy, Hungary, Cyprus, Romania, the UK and Portugal. Danish police investigated a threat against Copenhagen airport but the airport said it was operating normally.

blocks.caption: Danish police investigate renewed threats at Copenhagen airport. Photograph: Tom Little/Reuters

blocks.text: The warnings followed separate threats on Tuesday and Thursday that forced at least 35 flights to be diverted or searched, raising questions over an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos for travellers.

The latest threats affected at least nine flights to and from Prague, four flights over France, two flights en route to Sofia and a flight from Lisbon to Rome. Hungary scrambled fighter jets three times to escort civilian flights in its airspace, the defence minister, Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, said on Facebook.

The affected flights had knock-on effects but were a tiny percentage – just 0.0674% – of the 26,709 flights that according to the air traffic control agency Eurocontrol were scheduled in Europe on Friday.
A separate spate of threats on Friday against media organisations in Ireland disrupted broadcasts and prompted staff evacuations and police searches of offices and newsrooms.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, told RTÉ Radio 1 after it resumed scheduled broadcasting that such threats had to be taken seriously and were an effort to sow fear and anxiety.

blocks.caption: Police in Ireland investigate after a spate of threats against media organisations. Photograph: Natalia Campos/Reuters

blocks.text: “It shows how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and undermine the normal operation of society.” European security agencies would seek to identify those responsible and hold them accountable, said Martin.
The British broadcaster ⁠Sky said on Friday it had also received a ⁠security threat and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
Earlier this week, cyber-attacks targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

Investigators have said there was no evidence that hoaxes against airlines and other targets were being orchestrated by a hostile terror group or state actor, such as Russia or Iran, but that inquiries continue.
Some of the threats on Thursday were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a reference to a Russian far-right, ultranationalist and misogynistic movement founded in 2016.
Some officials suspect the waves of disruption are linked to European support for Ukraine in its war against the Russian invasion.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, said authorities needed more time to identify culprits but that there appeared to be a pattern. “It ⁠cannot be mere coincidence that so many incidents with exactly the same modus operandi are happening across Europe,” he told the national broadcaster TVE.
“The ​most reasonable assumption is that we are facing ​an attempt at hybrid aggression and a form ​of psychological warfare,” he said, adding that Europe must be prepared for more such challenges.

articles.title: Zambia's civil service overhaul raises questions
articles.summary: Government-backed retirements and institutional realignments are fueling debate in Zambia, with opposition politicians questioning transparency while officials defend the changes as necessary reforms.

image.caption: Opposition lawmakers have questioned the retirements and dismissals taking place across public institutionsImage: Han Xu/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Many people living in Zambia seek careers in the civil service because of the stability and security traditionally associated with government employment. But recent retirements, dismissals and restructuring exercises across several public institutions have unsettled that perception and sparked a national debate about the government's use of "national interest" provisions.

Among those affected is former police public relations officer Godfrey Chilabi, whose departure from the Zambia Police Service was announced in October. Choosing not to publicly discuss the circumstances surrounding his exit, Chilabi simply told local media that he had been retired in the national interest.
"Yes, I have been retired in national interest. I can't give any reason, but know I'm in retirement."
Chilabi's departure came amid a series of changes affecting public institutions in Zambia.

Charity Munganga, a Zambia Police Service deputy inspector general, was dismissed, and all staff members at the Zambia Medicines and Medical Supplies Agency were let go as part of a "reset" following a government audit.
Additionally, all directors in senior management at the Zambia Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) were put on administrative leave to facilitate an institutional realignment exercise.

The affected ZEMA directors will be assessed for their competence, performance and suitability for their positions before a final decision is made on whether they will be reinstated or separated from the institution, according to an October 20 statement by the Ministry of Green Economy and Environment cited by news portal Mwebantu.
Public servants on edge

The issue moved to the center of public debate in October when opposition lawmakers questioned the government in Parliament over retirements and dismissals taking place across public institutions following Zambia's August 2026 general election.
Can Zambia trust election referee?

Governance and political commentator Andrew Nguvu told DW that retirements carried out in the national interest raise important questions about transparency, fairness and the protection of a professional public service.
"If at all, there are legitimate reasons for retiring any particular civil servant, then obviously the government should clearly explain [these reasons]," Nguvu told DW.
He argued that public institutions should operate according to established procedures and the law rather than political considerations that could undermine institutional independence.

Zambian law allows service commissions to retire established officers in the national interest under provisions governing public service employment. Previous governments have also used the measure. However, the current exercise has generated significant scrutiny because it is occurring alongside broader restructuring efforts affecting multiple institutions.
Opposition cries hypocrisy

Critics argue that the issue is particularly sensitive because Zambia's ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) previously opposed the use of retirements in the national interest while in opposition.
As a result, opposition lawmakers, led by Stephen Kampyongo, have criticized the measures, which they view as inconsistent with the ruling party's earlier position.

Kampyongo, speaking during Vice President's Question Time in the National Assembly on October 17, asked what assurances the government was giving public servants "working in fear" and what measures were being taken to ensure those retired in the national interest did not become destitute.
Government pushes back

Responding on behalf of the government, Vice President Mutale Nalumango rejected suggestions that the exercise amounted to a political purge and instead described it as part of a lawful process of institutional realignment.
She acknowledged concerns surrounding the changes while defending the government's authority to make personnel adjustments within the public service framework.

"As provided for in section 39 of the Public Service Pensions Act, there are situations that arise and people fall by the way side. [It is] unfortunate that a life was lost, but maybe it is an issue that public servants/public service workers must brace themselves for," she told Parliament.
Nalumango's comments have been cited by critics as evidence that additional changes could occur as the government continues restructuring public institutions.
The debate has also been amplified by comments from UPND National Youth Chairperson Gilbert Liswaniso, who argued that governments naturally seek to work with people aligned with their vision.
"Every political party [that] comes to power, has to flush out! [It] has to work with the people aligned with the vision of that political party!"
Zambian youth find new opportunities in agriculture
For critics, such statements reinforce concerns that political considerations may be influencing decisions within the public service.
Civil rights activist David Chishimba rejects the notion that perceived political affiliation should determine a person's future in government employment.

"The Constitution, however, is very clear on this. It restricts public officers from participating in partisan politics while in office. This safeguards an impartial civil service. However, it does not prohibit private political belief or otherwise," he told DW.
Chishimba added that civil servants serve the country rather than any political organization. "Civil servants serve Zambia, not a party, the president or a campaign."
Workers face uncertainty
For public workers caught in the middle of these administrative realignments, the shift is deeply unsettling, noted Nguvu, the political commentator.
The measures come amid high living costs and household debt burdens in Zambia.
According to Nguvu, abrupt personnel changes can affect morale throughout the public service and leave workers uncertain about their professional future.
"This can weaken morale and help to destroy institutional memory. Most of these decisions lack clear explanations," he said.
Nguvu argued that concerns become more acute when explanations for personnel decisions are not communicated clearly.
The reported dismissals have also raised concerns among civil society groups about due process and accountability.
Chishimba, who is also president of the Zambia Council of Activists (ZACA), called for greater transparency from the authorities.

"ZACA respectfully calls on the Government to publish the names and evidence of those facing dismissal, submit every case to due process, and allow the Civil Service Commission to assert its constitutional independence."

articles.title: What to know about the IIHF Women's Ice Hockey World Championship
articles.summary: As ice hockey's governing body continues to wrangle over how to respond to a CAS order to reinstate Russia to international play, the top women's tournament gets underway in Denmark. Without Russia.

image.caption: The Women's Ice Hockey World Championship is being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to 16Image: Tomi Hänninen/Newspix24/IMAGO

blocks.text: Why is the tournament being held in November?

Since it's inception in 1990, the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship has almost always been held in the spring – apart from 2021 and 2022, when the COVID pandemic saw it moved to the summer. This year, though, the tournament, being hosted by Denmark from November 6 to November 16, is being held in November for the first time. The idea is make it easier for all of the world's best players to participate. Since its inception in 2023, the North America-based Professional Women's Hockey League (PWHL), widely considered the world's best, has had to pause its season to allow its players to take part in the Worlds. This is no longer necessary, as the PWHL's regular season doesn't open until December.

"This gives the women's game a unique selling point," International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) President Franz Reindl recently told the SID news agency. "Because the PWHL season begins after this, we can be certain that the very best players are participating."
How has the tournament format changed?

Previously, the teams were divided into a stronger group and a weaker group, with the idea being to avoid, as much as possible, lopsided scores. This is because women's hockey is not as balanced as the men's game, with Canada or the United States having won every tournament since its inception. Under the old system, all five teams in the stronger Group A advanced to the quarterfinals. Under the new format, four of the five teams advance from both groups. This also sees the two powerhouses, the USA and Canada in separate groups, meaning the marquis matchup can't occur early in the tournament.
Group A: USA, Czechia, Switzerland, Germany, Austria
Group B: Canada, Finland, Sweden, Japan, Denmark
Will Russia be competing at this tournament?

No. While the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled on October 30, 2026 – a week before the opening faceoff of the Women's Ice Hockey World Championship – that the IIHF must allow Russia back into its tournaments during the 2026-2027 season, it made no mention of this tournament. Under the CAS ruling though, the IIHF will be required to include Russia at the 2027 tournament in Quebec City.
Who are the contenders?

As noted above, either Canada or the United States has won every edition of this tournament – and indeed the two countries have split Olympic gold medals between them (Canada 5, USA 3) since the sport was introduced to the Winter Games in 1998. There is nothing to suggest that this is about to change in Herning and Esbjerg, although Canada enters the tournament with a vastly different roster from the one that won Olympic silver in Milano in February. Among those looking to break this North American domination are Finland, the only other team ever to have made it to a World Championship final and Switzerland, who took bronze in Milano.
Why are the USA and Canada not wearing their traditional uniforms?

The United States and Canada are having to play in generic kits provided by the International Ice Hockey Federation's official supplier due to an ongoing commercial rights dispute. The Canadian federation, Hockey Canada, said in a statement on Wednesday that its players would be wearing jerseys designed by True Hockey instead of their Bauer jerseys featuring the national team logo. USA Hockey has confirmed that its players too will be wearing jerseys without its national emblem.
"While we have yet to see the jersey Canada will be playing in on Friday, our team remains focused on the tournament and representing our country proudly on and off the ice,” Hockey Canada said.

articles.title: Global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels in 2026, likely the second-warmest year on record
articles.summary: Climate scientists say the world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree Celsius threshold in 2026. This year is also on track to become the second-warmest on record.

image.caption: United Nations officially assumes that the 1.5 degree target will be overshotImage: Andre Penner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Global temperatures will almost certainly average more than 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels in 2026, the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service said Friday.
That would make 2026 the second calendar year after 2024 above the threshold set as part of the Paris Agreement.
What does the 1.5-degree target mean?
The Paris treaty was aimed at preventing global temperatures from rising above 1.5 degrees Celsius in the long term. The 2015 deal was seen as a major step forward in tackling climate change.
Most of the world's nations agreed to hold global temperature rise to well below 2 degrees Celsius compared to pre-industrial levels and "pursue efforts" to keep it below 1.5 degrees.
The target concerns long-term warming, so a single year above 1.5 degrees does not in itself mean it has been breached.
Could 2026 become the warmest year on record?
Copernicus estimates that 2026 will most likely be the second-warmest year after 2024 since records began. However, there is a 20% chance that it could surpass 2024 levels.
Ten years on: Has the Paris climate deal delivered?
The climate service also expects the four-year average for 2023 to 2026 to be above the 1.5 degree threshold.

October 2026 was the warmest October on record globally, with an average global surface temperature of 1.75 degrees above pre-industrial levels for the month. It marked the third consecutive month above the 1.5 degrees threshold.

"An exceptionally strong El Nino is adding further heat to a climate already warmed by human activities, while 2026 is on track to become the second calendar year above 1.5 degrees," said Samantha Burgess of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
That goal is no longer within reach
The UN Environment Programme now expects warming to overshoot the Paris Agreement's 1.5-degree target.
Because this threatens drastic climate extremes and dangerous tipping points, the overshoot should be kept as small and short as possible, it said.

blocks.caption: Burning fossil fuels is one of the main drivers of climate changeImage: Gerald Herbert/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to a September report by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP), every additional fraction of a degree makes the risks and impacts worse.
Climate scientist Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, called for temperatures to be lowered quickly again by removing CO2 from the atmosphere.

UNEP lays out a scenario in which the world sees warming peak at 1.7 to 1.8 degrees Celsius around mid-century, before falling back to 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2100. Getting there would require steep emissions cuts of 69% by 2040, relative to 2025 levels.
It was now unavoidable that global warming would exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within the next five years, Rockström said at a briefing.
He said that humanity was currently on "a path to an unmanageable future."
