articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago
articles.summary:
Far-right politician speaks to Conservative Political Action Conference and makes unsubstantiated claims about election fraud

Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.

On Thursday night Bolsonaro made his first major public appearance since arriving in the US, speaking at a rightwing gathering at Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property where he claimed “great things” were still to come.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro arriving in Miami after fleeing Brazil last week. Photograph: Marta Lavandier/AP

blocks.text: “I know this wasn’t the end for Brazil and I know it wasn’t the end for America,” Bolsonaro, 45, told a gala dinner at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC)’s four-day “gathering of visionaries” event, where the former British prime minister Liz Truss is also due to speak.

“Even when what seems like the end isn’t what we’d hoped for, we must thank God and have even more faith that this isn’t yet the end,” he added. “No one shuts the door that he opens – and the door he shuts, no one opens.”
Earlier, in his first post-election interview, Bolsonaro made a series of unsubstantiated claims about election fraud and insisted he received “help from absolutely no one” to flee.

“It was all me,” Bolsonaro told the New York Times, contradicting reports that he was helped by the Trump adviser Jason Miller and Santiago Caputo, a close aide to Argentina’s rightwing president, Javier Milei.

He said he would “take to the grave” the full story of how he fled Brazil, where he faces federal police investigations for money laundering and corruption. Bolsonaro is a member of congress who has held elected office for more than 20 years but he will lose parliamentary immunity early next year when his term ends, meaning he could then be prosecuted.

blocks.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro and his brother Eduardo in the US, where both now live in self-imposed exile.  Photograph: Eduardo Bolsonaro/Instagram/Reuters

blocks.text: Brazilian analysts agree that by skipping the country after an election in which he received 59m votes, Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, abdicated leadership of the opposition and sabotaged his political future.

Thomas Traumann, an author and pundit for the TV network GloboNews, said: “Flávio was foolish enough to throw away the leadership of the opposition that he could have exercised had he stayed in Brazil. But the [Bolsonaro] family is still a player.”

Flávio Bolsonaro’s brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro, also lives in self-imposed exile in the US and will have to serve a four-year sentence for coercion if he returns to Brazil. Four other members of the Bolsonaro family were elected to congress in last month’s election, including their brothers Carlos and Jair Renan and stepmother, Michelle Bolsonaro.

blocks.caption: Michelle Bolsonaro, the former first lady of Brazil, was elected to congress last month along with three other members of the Bolsonaro family. Photograph: André Penner/AP

blocks.text: Traumann believed it was not inconceivable that Jair Bolsonaro would attempt a political comeback if he managed to negotiate his way out of his 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. However, as things stand, the 71-year-old is banned from running for office until 2060 and must live under house arrest.
after newsletter promotion
Many doubt the Bolsonaro family can continue to control Bolsonarismo, the populist political movement that takes their name, with two key members in exile and one imprisoned.
“[The movement] is mortally wounded because of its mistakes and its crimes,” the political scientist Sérgio Abranches told the newspaper O Globo this week.

Abranches said democratic rightwing politicians now had a chance to “detach” themselves from the Bolsonaros’ anti-democratic movement and break off in a new direction before the next presidential election in 2030.
Flávio Bolsonaro told the New York Times he would “obviously” be a candidate in future elections but said his future lay in the US “at least for now”.

blocks.caption: A campaign rally for Flávio Bolsonaro shortly before the presidential election runoff last month.  Photograph: Raquel Cunha/Reuters

blocks.text: It is unclear where Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been granted a US visa by Trump, will live. His brother Eduardo set up home in Southlake, Texas, after leaving Brazil last year – although some expect him to move after the traditionally conservative state elected the Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor in this week’s midterms.

In a video posted on CPAC’s social networks before Thursday’s event, Eduardo Bolsonaro played down the risk posed by the “blue tsunami” to their ability to stay in the US. “They [Democrats] will try [to make trouble for us] – but it’s not up to Congress … to revoke visas or citizenships,” he said.
Likening their plight to that of a female asylum seeker fleeing Iran for fear of being killed after refusing to wear a hijab, he added: “I am 100% legal – as is my brother and his family.”

articles.title: Kenyan cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years in prison for murder of 190 children
articles.summary: A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children starved to death on his orders and buried in a forest, among 500 suspected victims…

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie, a Kenyan cult leader accused of ordering his followers, who were members of the Good News International Church, to starve themselves to death in Shakahola Forest, looks on in court on Friday following his sentencing at the Mombasa High Court, in Kenya. (Monicah Mwangi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children starved to death on his orders and buried in a forest, among 500 suspected victims of one of the worst ceremonial massacres of modern times.
Prosecutors say he told followers of his apocalyptic Christian church to starve themselves to death
The sentence was comprised of 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, Justice Diana Kavedza said, reading out the judgment.

Prosecutors said Mackenzie, who led an apocalyptic Christian church in a forest near eastern Kenya's Indian Ocean coast, had told his followers to starve themselves to death, along with their children, to reach heaven before the end of the world.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

items: Kenyan cult leader faces 191 murder charges in child mass starvation deaths

blocks.text: Mackenzie, wearing a grey polo shirt and black trousers, smiled as he entered a tent set up outside the court where the hearing was held.
He had denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve. The court rejected his defence.
Father lost 6 children
The case shocked Kenya in April 2023 when police began uncovering bodies in Shakahola Forest near the coastal town of Malindi.
Although only the cases of 190 children and one adult victim were covered by the trial, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights says 448 bodies were ultimately found in the forest.

Mackenzie is also accused of ordering the deaths of 52 people found at a separate location in a village 30 kilometres away, bringing the suspected total toll to 500. He has pleaded not guilty in that case.

The scale of the killing is comparable to that of a doomsday cult that killed more than 700 people in Uganda in 2000, and the 1978 Jonestown massacre in Guyana when an American cult leader killed more than 900 people by ordering them to drink poison.
Paul black trousers. The Kenyan cult leader smiled as he entered a tent set up outside the court earlier, ahead of his hearing. (Monicah Mwangi/Reuters)
Stephen Mwiti, 48, father of six of Mackenzie's child victims and husband of one of his convicted accomplices, said his wife had taken the children to Shakahola where they were starved to death.
Even if the adults had agreed to fast, "what about the children?" Mwiti told Reuters ahead of the sentencing.

"I lost children and I will not be able to get them back no matter what happens to Mackenzie and his accomplices," Mwiti said. "I expect him to be sentenced to death or be jailed for life so that he never comes out to cause more deaths."
Dan Mackenzie, one of Paul's sons, said his father did not spare his own family.

"I didn't end up in Shakahola, because I didn't believe anymore about ... going to heaven. So I left the church and started doing my own thing," he told Reuters. "I lost friends, too, and my younger brother. It's justice to the people who we lost over there in Shakahola."
Calls for more accountability

Mackenzie had been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie's church in Malindi and he relocated to the nearby Shakahola Forest.

The discoveries prompted calls for tighter oversight of religious groups. Kenyan President William Ruto appointed a task force in May 2023 to review the legal and regulatory framework, and separate government-backed and Senate proposals were published in 2024, though they have yet to be passed into law.

Ojiro Odhiambo, head of rapid response at the Kenya Human Rights Commission, said the conviction was an important step but accountability should go further as local administrators, police, intelligence officers and religious leaders bore responsibility for failing to act on repeated warning signs.
"All these people have failed the people," he said.
In 2023, Ruto said he took responsibility as president for the government having failed to prevent the deaths.

articles.title: ‘Profound anger’ among black voters over Kemi Badenoch’s slavery remarks
articles.summary:
Operation Black Vote chair says Tory leader’s claim that Britain should not apologise has caused ‘hurt and disbelief’

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt…

blocks.text: The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, has caused “profound anger, hurt and disbelief” among many black voters with her comments about transatlantic slavery, according to the chair of Operation Black Vote (OBV), who urged the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to apologise for Britain’s involvement without delay.

David Weaver, a former government adviser, said the Labour and Tory leaders risked alienating black voters with their handling of the issue of a state apology for slavery, while saying Badenoch’s remarks showed a “troubling absence of moral leadership”.

In a week in which the UK political agenda was dominated by postcolonial legacies, Badenoch said Burnham should not apologise for Britain’s historical role in slavery “because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash”, while criticising Commonwealth leaders on X.

Burnham, while saying he was open to making a formal apology on behalf of the British state, has ruled out reparations. Weaver said he welcomed the prime minister’s apparent willingness to apologise, but said the government’s “almost reflexive insistence” that any apology must come with assurances “reparations are off the table” was concerning.

blocks.caption: David Weaver, the chair of Operation Black Vote. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Weaver said only the prime minister had the power to address the hurt felt by descendant communities and show Britain had the “moral courage to apologise without qualification”.
But he said Badenoch’s comments highlighted wider concerns about the UK’s political climate, adding: “At Operation Black Vote, we are hearing profound anger, hurt and disbelief.”

He added: “For us, this is not an abstract historical debate. It concerns our families, our heritage and our humanity. Political leaders should not underestimate the depth of feeling within black communities or their democratic power.”
Weaver said that in seeking an apology, Commonwealth nations wanted recognition of continuing colonial legacies that hampered development, and that Badenoch’s comments were “profoundly insulting”.

This week marked the second anniversary of Badenoch becoming the first black woman to lead a major British political party. OBV, a national, non-partisan civil rights group founded in 1996, welcomed her historic achievement in becoming Tory leader in 2024.

Meanwhile, although black voters were more likely than any other voters to have backed Labour in the 2024 general election, Weaver said OBV had found they felt “despondent” with the party and “taken for granted”, in particular over its handling of the consequences of the Windrush scandal.

Weaver added: “All parties should understand that to not apologise for slavery, the worst crime against humanity, is an insult. An apology should not have to be begged for. It should be an expression of genuine remorse and moral responsibility, not a carefully managed political statement designed to demonstrate toughness or avoid obligation.

“Reparative justice is not just about money. Ending an injustice does not erase responsibility for perpetrating it. We must ask why acknowledging this particular historical injustice remains so difficult and whether deeper racial attitudes continue to shape the debate.”
after newsletter promotion

Badenoch, who has advocated a “colour-blind” approach to race, has long argued that people from ethnic minorities should be free to express differing views on race without being accused of betraying their communities. But while attempting to frame herself as a unifier, Badenoch has given roles to the hard-right politician Rupert Lowe, Katie Lam – the MP who said a “large number” of legal migrants “need to go home” – and the former neo-Nazi Joshua Bonehill-Paine, while outlining plans to scrap the public sector equality duty and leave the European court of human rights.

Weaver said: “She’s the leader of the Conservative party. That’s a big deal. She’s got a high popularity rating and can be very effective. But many black voters tell us there’s a lot of mistrust for her lack of empathy – and because she will sometimes say things her white counterparts could not say and get away with it. So she becomes the front for unacceptable views on race.

“The current state of public discourse – and the silence when it comes to challenging it – contributes to a sense among black communities that they are being treated with contempt across the political spectrum.

“This is not just about Badenoch. Just because you’re black doesn’t mean you have to hold a particular point of view. But your heritage, whether you are white or black, does not place your views beyond challenge. An apology for slavery is about humanity and decency and seeing people’s worth. Andy Burnham must do the right thing – and soon.”
Downing Street and the Conservative party were approached for comment. Commonwealth leaders have said the UK has agreed to “structured dialogue” in the next year.

articles.title: Palace says water supply remains sufficient amid El Niño
articles.summary: Malacañang said on Friday that water supplies remain sufficient despite the ongoing El Niño phenomenon.

blocks.text: Published November 6, 2026 9:00pm
Malacañang said on Friday that water supplies remain sufficient despite the ongoing El Niño phenomenon.
Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said that there is already a very strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific.

“Tinitiyak po ng pamahalaan na sapat ang suplay ng tubig sa mga dams at mga water sources. Noong November 3, nasa 208.70 meters ang lebel ng tubig sa Angat Dam, mas mataas sa minimum operating level na 180 meters,” Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said.

(The government guarantees that there are enough water supplies in the dam and water resources. On November 3, there were 208.70 meters of water in Angat Dam, which is higher than the minimum operating level of 180 meters.)
Castro said that the Department of Agriculture has also guaranteed a sufficient supply of food, especially rice. The Department of Energy said that it was ensuring the maintenance of power plants.

“Sabi nga ng Pangulo, ibang klase ang very strong El Niño na nararanasan natin at mararanasan pa sa mga susunod na araw pero handa po ang gobyerno na tugunan ang pangangailangan ng ating mga kababayan,” Castro said.
(As the President said, this very strong El Niño is a different class that we will experience in the coming days, but the government is ready to attend to the needs of our countrymen.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Iranians face looming war threat with no reliable info
articles.summary: Ordinary people living in Iran have little idea of the course of the war and peace talks on the global stage. With few sources of information, they are forced to navigate conflicting rumors and fears…

image.caption: Fears of a new US attack are rising again in Iran with US midterms no longer a factor for Donald TrumpImage: Majid Asgaripour/WANA/REUTERS

blocks.text: "There is a constant sense of fear in the air. Every time I hear a loud noise, I flinch. Even when a door slams, I jump, thinking that bombs are falling," said a 37-year-old mother living in Tehran.
Unlike in the opening months of the war, her children are going to school.
"I don't work, but keeping the children at home out of fear is not a solution," she told DW. "They would go stir-crazy in our small apartment."
Iran's government takes aim at 'rumors'

Schools remain open across Iran despite the military standoff with the US and Israel. However, some parents whose children attend private schools have received messages from those schools explaining what to do in the event of a renewed war or other emergency.
Numerous parents have shared such messages on social media.
The country's Ministry of Education has tried to reassure the public.
Strike on Iran school: Did US commit a war crime?
"People should not pay attention to rumors spread with the aim of sowing fear and forcing schools to close," Ali Farhadi, a ministry spokesperson, said in a recent media interview.

He said the ministry will decide whether the schools stay open or close, and will do so in coordination with the security authorities. Should the security outlook change, the situation will be reassessed accordingly, the official said.
'Pickaxe Mountain' at the center of nuclear attack fears
Parallel to Farhadi's appeal to disregard rumors aimed at raising fear, state media themselves are discussing scenarios of a possible nuclear attack.

On November 2, Iranian state television broadcast an advisory on protective measures in case of a nuclear strike. People were advised to remain in a shelter for at least 24 hours in the event of such an emergency.

Specifically, many in Iran fear the US is preparing to use nuclear weapons against Iran's "Pickaxe Mountain" underground bunker located some 220 kilometers (140 miles) south of Tehran. US President Donald Trump has hinted at attacking the location, which is close to Iran's Natanz nuclear facility, but made no explicit mention of using nuclear weapons.
Iranian government denies that any work related to its nuclear program is being carried out at the mountain bunker.

The fighting between the US and Iran has mostly petered out in recent months as the Trump administration focused on the midterm election. But two days after the election, on November 5, the US news outlet Axios reported that the US military was making final preparations for a possible resumption of large-scale strikes against Iran.
Trump still has months before new Congress takes power
At the same time, there are also hopes that a Democrat-controlled Congress would force Trump to scale down his military ambitions.

"It is still difficult to make any concrete assessment of the implications of the US midterm election results for the war with Iran," writes Hamidreza Azizi, Senior Fellow and Iran expert at the International Crisis Group, in response to a request from DW.

Azizi says the Iranian leadership sees the election results as their own victory. The regime's resistance to the Trump administration has contributed to the Republican Party's loss in the US midterms, and some in Tehran are already seeking to frame the result as a sort of revenge for the US-Israeli assassination of senior Iranian leaders in the opening stages of the war.
Against this backdrop, Iran is likely to take an even harder line on its core demands.

At the same time, Azizi points out that Trump has at least two months before the new Congress officially takes office. He could decide to resume strikes on Iran in an attempt to offset a domestic political setback by targeting a foreign policy victory.
Republicans rebuke Trump on Iran war, economy after midterm wipeout
Reporters kept in the dark on peace talks

For now, Qatari mediators are trying to persuade Tehran and Washington to agree on a draft peace deal. The aim is to prevent another round of escalation and pave the way for the resumption of direct talks in the coming days.
But even well-connected journalists in Iran have little information on the substance of the talks, which are closed to the public.

In a post on X on October 31, Iranian journalist Hadi Mohammadi wrote: "Domestic media outlets are completely in the dark about negotiations that directly affect people's everyday lives. They have to wait for reports from Axios, Al Arabiya, Al Jazeera and other international media outlets. In such an environment, developing our own narratives and doing journalism becomes pointless."
As the fog of war persists, many in Iran no longer have the energy to keep up with the media reporting. A 72-year-old retired woman from western Iran told DW she now deliberately avoids the news.
"I hardly have the strength to think about it anymore. I'm just glad that my three children have emigrated," she said.
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: UK house prices fall at steepest rate in more than three years
articles.summary: October drop of 0.6% leaves average price of property at £296,285, says Lloyds, as high mortgage rates hit market

blocks.text: UK house prices fell at the steepest rate in more than three years in October, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline, as high mortgage rates hit the housing market.

The average price of a typical UK property stood at £296,285 last month as prices unexpectedly dropped 0.6% compared with September, the steepest fall since the lender Lloyds recorded a 1.6% drop in August 2023.
Analysts had expected a small monthly rise of 0.1%, which would have marked the first monthly increase since June.
House prices were down 1.2% compared with the same month last year, the biggest annual fall since October 2023.

“Housing demand is currently being tested by a challenging economic backdrop,” said Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds. “Renewed inflationary pressures, driven in part by the conflict in the Middle East, are keeping borrowing costs high and adding to the squeeze on household finances, making some buyers understandably more cautious.”

Prospective buyers are facing increasingly high borrowing costs, with the average two-year fixed mortgage running at 5.97% and the average five-year fixed rate at 5.99%, according to the latest Moneyfacts market update.

The figures come a day after the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee put up the base rate by a quarter of a point to 4%, the first increase in three years, to fight inflationary pressure caused by the Iran war.
The conflict in the Middle East has driven the price of oil above $100 a barrel in recent months, resulting in soaring fuel prices and pushing inflation to 3.5% in September.

“The market has lost some momentum as we head towards the end of the year,” said Amy Reynolds, the head of sales at the Richmond estate agency Antony Roberts. “Buyers are still out there, but they’re being careful. The people hit hardest are those remortgaging and second-steppers trying to stretch to one more bedroom.
“The real damage is psychological. Another rise tells people that borrowing is getting more expensive, not cheaper, and that makes them hesitate.”

The property services company Savills this week said Britain’s sluggish housing market was not expected to recover until 2028, when a forecast improvement in the economy and mortgage affordability are expected to support a recovery.
While annual house price growth remains relatively strong in Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales, there is growing pressure in the south of England.
Greater London recorded the largest annual decline in October, with prices falling 3.1% year on year to an average of £524,892.
The capital was followed by the south-east and south-west of England, which recorded annual declines of 2.4% last month, to £379,258 and £298,057 respectively.
after newsletter promotion

On Friday the online property portal Rightmove downgraded its expectations of revenue and profit growth to the lower end of its guidance amid a slowdown in the housing market, in results for the four months to 31 October.
It said that high mortgage rates had resulted in buyer demand falling by 10%, with agreed sales down 9%, as record numbers of homes on the market led to “some downward pressure” on house prices.

Rightmove said there had been an increase in inquiries per property in the rental market, with prices up 2.9% year on year, but there were 6% fewer new homes on the website compared with the end of last year.
Last month, the Bank of England released figures showing that the number of home mortgage approvals fell to 53,443 in September, the lowest monthly figure since December 2023.
Last week, Nationwide reported that house prices flatlined in October, with the annual rate of growth dropping to the slowest in more than two years.

“The path back to growth runs through rate stability, and that road just got a little longer,” said Anthony Codling, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets. “On balance, this report is cautiously negative for near-term sentiment but does not signal a structural collapse.”

articles.title: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
articles.summary: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.

blocks.text: The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe.

The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.

Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.

It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.

Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".

One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes, external.

One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.

As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.

"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.
Additional reporting by Davide Ghiglione

articles.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
articles.summary:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s…

blocks.text: The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts, uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs.
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

articles.title: New bomb threats target Irish media, more European flights
articles.summary: Newsrooms have been evacuated across Ireland after another wave of bomb threats. Dublin is hosting a high-level EU meeting in several days.

image.caption: RTE had to turn to mostly pre-recorded shows after staff were told to leave the buildingImage: Natalia Campos/REUTERS

blocks.text: Following days of bomb threats grounding flights across Europe, media institutions in Ireland and the UK were added to the list of targets on Friday.
Irish public broadcaster Raidio Teilifis Eirean (RTE) said that its buildings had been evacuated after receiving a bomb threat. Other media organizations were also taking security measures.
The threats come two days before Dublin, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, hosts a high-level meeting with other bloc members.
An RTE reporter said the group that claimed to be behind Friday's bomb threats was the same that had sent threats to airlines earlier in the week.
UK-based broadcaster Sky also said it had received a "security threat" on Friday.
What did Irish officials say about bomb threats against media networks?
"We don't yet know whether it's an individual behind this effort, or some form of a co-ordinated effort," Irish Deputy Prime Minister Simon Harris told Cork 96FM radio.
He said it was a "serious and evolving situation."
Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin called the developments "worrying," but said the Gardai (Irish police) and Defense Forces were looking into who was behind the threats.
He also urged any organization that receives a similar threat to take it seriously and report it to the police so they can have a "picture of what's happening."

"It just illustrates how relatively simple it can be to cause disruption and to undermine the normal operation of society through unconventional activities of this kind, which are designed to cause disruption, designed to cause fear and anxiety," RTE cited Martin as saying.

Asked about any possible connection with the European Union meetings coming up in Dublin, the prime minister, also known as the Taoiseach, said it was important to maintain the ability to let such meetings go ahead.
"We have the largest number of prime ministers ever at the one time in our country, and that does call for very significant security operations."
Further bomb threats made to flights
More than two dozen flights were affected by threats this week, with further incidents reported on Friday.
Police in Denmark and the Czech Republic responded to threats that ultimately proved to be false.
A flight operated by the Romanian carrier Tarom going from Prague to Bucharest received a threat, but landed at its intended destination before officials deemed it false.

Police in Copenhagen said they had been to the airport for the second day in a row "in connection with threats directed at air traffic" but that there had been no danger to passengers or disruption to flights.

While bomb threats are not uncommon, such a wave of threats being made in a short period of time is unusual, especially amid increasing geopolitical tensions with Russia and a wave of hybrid attacks that have brought disruption to Europe.

articles.title: Former U of Manitoba law dean accused of fraud loses bid to fight extradition from France
articles.summary: Jonathan Black-Branch has lost his bid to avoid extradition from France to Canada to face fraud charges.

image.caption: Jonathan Black-Branch disappeared from Canada before he was disbarred by the Law Society of Manitoba in 2024. He was arrested in France where a court has supported his extradition. (University of Manitoba)

blocks.text: Manitoba
Jonathan Black-Branch has lost his bid to avoid extradition from France to Canada to face fraud charges.
Jonathan Black-Branch was arrested in a Paris suburb in April
A French court on Friday ruled in support of the request.

The 64-year-old former dean of the University of Manitoba's law school in Winnipeg is accused of misusing more than $600,000 from the university to pay his bills, buy pricey meals at a members-only club and spend on his education at Ivy League schools.
He was under an international arrest warrant issued when found in Neuilly-sur-Seine, a suburb just west of Paris in April. The extradition request was issued in May.
Black-Branch appeared in the Versailles Court of Appeal three weeks ago, arguing against his extradition. The court reserved its decision to Nov. 6.
No date has been given for when the extradition will take place.

items: French court to decide next month on extradition for former U of Manitoba law dean accused of fraud
Professor hopes former University of Manitoba law dean will 'be held to account' after overseas arrest

blocks.text: Black-Branch was hired as U of M's law dean in 2016 but abruptly left the post in 2020 and moved to Europe amidst an internal investigation by the university into financial mismanagement.
Later that year, the University of Southampton in the U.K. announced Black-Branch as the new head of its law school. He is originally from England and was called to the bar there in 1995.
Days later, though, the university changed course and announced it would no longer be hiring him.

In 2023, a months-long law hearing by the Law Society of Manitoba found Black-Branch had committed professional misconduct and the U of M asked Winnipeg police to investigate criminal charges, but his whereabouts were unknown by then.
The Law Society of Manitoba disbarred him in 2024 and fined him $36,000.
The same year, the U of M sued Black-Branch and he was ordered in a default judgment to pay nearly $680,000 and more than $3,000 in costs, plus three per cent annual interest.
The Bar Standards Board for England and Wales has since barred him from practising law there, too, citing his actions in Manitoba as "blatant and sustained dishonesty."

items: Disgraced former Manitoba law dean racked up millions in Swiss debt ahead of France arrest, documents suggest
Law dean facing extradition to Canada taught at German for-profit school for years

blocks.text: During his time in Europe Black-Branch had been working at Germany's largest university for several years.
He was a lecturer at the for-profit IU International University of Applied Sciences from late 2021 until mid-2025, school spokesperson Christin Eitner told CBC News in October.
Black-Branch also sought to be naturalized as a Swiss citizen in late 2023, though it was unclear as to whether he completed that process.
Documents show he racked up about $5.6 million in debt in Switzerland, most of it tied to real estate.

Darren Bernhardt has been with CBC Manitoba since 2009 and specializes in offbeat and local history stories. He is the author of two bestselling books: The Lesser Known: A History of Oddities from the Heart of the Continent, and Prairie Oddities: Punkinhead, Peculiar Gravity and More Lesser Known Histories.

articles.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production as Elon Musk focuses on robotics and AI
articles.summary:
Decision made in order for factory in Texas to be used for Cybercab, the carmaker’s self-driving taxi

Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking…

blocks.text: Elon Musk has announced that Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck, marking the end of a failed effort to take a chunk of the lucrative market for pickups in the US.

The billionaire chief executive said production of the car would stop in about the middle of next year at the company’s factory in Texas in order to use the plant for the Cybercab, its self-driving taxi.
Musk did not say whether Tesla had plans to produce the vehicle in another factory, although that would probably require significant investment for the specialised tooling needed to make it.

Musk has pinned hopes for Tesla on robotics, artificial intelligence and an autonomous driving fleet rather than following the traditional carmakers’ approach of developing a steady stream of new models to entice private buyers.

It caps a tricky week for the world’s richest person, after Republican candidates he had backed with $446m (£332m) in donations lost in the US midterm elections. The paper value of Musk’s fortune fell by $113bn after the extent of the rout became clear, as stock market investors questioned whether a Democrat-led Congress could slow the pace of the AI boom.
Tesla shares fell by 11% on Thursday, while his AI and rocket launch company, SpaceX, dropped by 9%.

Tesla started deliveries of the Cybertruck in late 2023, after several long delays as the company tried to cope with the technical challenges of producing such an unusual vehicle – and particularly its steel shell.
The Cybertruck never made it on sale in Europe because it did not reach the required safety standards.

Even before sales began, Musk acknowledged how difficult it would be to make it a success. In a 2023 earnings call, he said: “We dug our own grave with Cybertruck,” and noted “enormous challenges” in increasing production and earning money from it.

Musk had said the company aimed to sell 200,000 Cybertrucks each year but it never approached that target. Tesla does not report sales of the trucks separately but in the third quarter of 2026 it delivered only 8,300 “other models”, which include the Cybertruck. The vast majority of its sales were the Model 3 saloon and the Model Y SUV, with 478,000 combined deliveries during the quarter.
Tesla also this year stopped production of its Model S and Model X, its premium saloon and SUV, amid declining sales for ageing products.
after newsletter promotion

Tesla’s automotive focus has shifted to the Cybercab. Tesla has started offering paid trips in the car, which has space for two passengers and no steering wheel, in limited parts of Austin, Texas. However, it is unclear how quickly the company will be able to roll out the taxi service around the US or further afield amid close regulatory scrutiny of driverless car technology.

As well as the Cybercab, Tesla is still ramping up production of its long-delayed Semi electric lorry. Musk is also aiming to produce one other new model: the Roadster sportscar, which Musk revealed with a demonstration of a “flying car” version that used thrusters developed by SpaceX to drive up a curved ramp before flipping and landing. Tesla is aiming to start production of a road-bound version in 2028. Analysts do not expect the Roadster to make a large difference to Tesla’s future profits.
Beyond vehicles, the Texas factory will also be used to build Tesla’s Optimus humanoid robot.

Musk posted on X, the social network he owns: “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

articles.title: SC upholds constitutionality of law extending Barangay, SK officials' terms
articles.summary: The Supreme Court (SC) has upheld the constitutionality of the law extending the term of office of Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years, while scheduling the next Barangay…

blocks.text: The Supreme Court (SC) has upheld the constitutionality of the law extending the term of office of Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials to five years, while scheduling the next Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) for November 2028.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Republic Act No. 12326 into law in September, which effectively postponed the BSKE, established the five-year term, and rescheduled the polls to 2028.
In a 33-page decision, the High Court dismissed the petition filed by election lawyer Romulo Macalintal challenging the constitutionality of the law.

The SC stated that the law's primary purpose is to set the term of office rather than to postpone the election, and therefore the guidelines established in the 2023 Macalintal decision—cited by the petitioner—do not apply.

“It sets a new five-year interval between elections. Its principal purpose, as gleaned from its text, is to fix the term of barangay and SK officials. Setting the next BSKE for November 2028 implements the new term, and is not an independent objective,” the decision read.

The High Court noted that rescheduling the BSKE to November 2028 merely implements the new term, adding that an adjustment to the election schedule does not automatically classify the legislation as an election postponement law.
The SC also underscored Congress's power to fix, modify, and extend the term of barangay officials as necessary, provided the transition period before the new term takes effect remains reasonable.

With incumbent barangay officials having been elected on October 30, 2023, the Court found the November 2028 schedule reasonable, not unduly long, and consistent with the five-year term prescribed under RA 12326.

Additionally, the Court considered lawmakers' concerns that conducting the BSKE in 2027 could disrupt the Commission on Elections’ preparations for the May 2028 National and Local Elections, while a five-year cycle starting in 2026 would cause future BSKEs to overlap with the 2031 national polls.

The High Court also rejected the argument that the law infringes upon the public's right to vote, emphasizing that the key requirement of suffrage is that elections take place regularly at fixed and predictable intervals established by law.

“Republic Act No. 12232 did not abolish or indefinitely postpone the BSKE but changed the statutory term and established a new and definite electoral cycle. We ruled that such legislation did not violate the right of suffrage,” the court said.

Finally, the SC clarified that the law does not grant incumbent officials a new term, but rather allows them to remain in office in a holdover capacity, which does not constitute a legislative appointment.

“The incumbents themselves were elected in the October 2023 BKSE. Their continuation in office pending the election of their successors is not an appointment by Congress, but the operation of a hold-over provision that the Court has repeatedly sustained,” the decision noted.

Macalintal previously filed a petition seeking the issuance of a temporary restraining order or a status quo ante order directing the Office of the President, through the Executive Secretary, the Senate, the House of Representatives, and the Commission on Elections (Comelec) to refrain from implementing RA No. 12326. He also asked the SC to declare the law inoperative, invalid, and/or unconstitutional insofar as it pertains to the postponement of the BSKE.

Accordingly, the SC denied Macalintal’s prayer for the issuance of a temporary restraining order, status quo ante order, and/or writ of preliminary injunction against the law, ultimately dismissing his petition for lack of merit.
The decision was penned by then Associate Justice Rodil V. Zalameda and promulgated on October 14, 2026.
Comelec
For its part, the Comelec expressed its appreciation for the prompt resolution of the issue, clearing any doubts about the constitutionality of the term-fixing law.

“Although not unanimous, the SC decision is already a jurisprudence forming part of the law of the land. Our deepest appreciation to the highest court for resolving promptly the controversy and clearing any doubt as to the legality of the law,” Comelec Chairman George Erwin Garcia told reporters in a message.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows
articles.summary: YouGov survey finds support for tree planting and emissions taxes but opposition to air travel and fuel levies

blocks.text: Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.

The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.

Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent and scientists say human-driven climate breakdown through the burning of fossil fuels is increasing the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and destructive storms.

Days before the Cop31 climate conference in Turkey, the polling showed vast majorities (79-89%) in Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK thought countries would combat the crisis more effectively by working internationally.

Those in the EU were more likely to say that climate action decisions should be made at EU rather than national level, a feeling shared by 50-54% of respondents in France, Italy and Germany as well as 61% in Denmark and 64% in Spain.

Majorities of between 65% and 83% in each country surveyed said they were worried about the climate crisis, including 23%-42% who were “very worried”. YouGov noted an uptick in concern during this summer’s heatwaves.
In April, 74% of respondents in France said they were worried about the climate crisis but that figure was up to 83% by mid-August and still at that level last month.

The number of French people who were “very worried” about climate change also rose, from 28% in April to a record high of 42% in August, a level it held last month. Concern in other countries spiked in August but has since dipped.

In Germany, for example, the number very concerned rose from 27% in April to 40% in August but has now fallen back to 31%. Concern remained relatively stable in Denmark, at 66%-69% “worried” and 20%-23% “very worried”.

Across the six countries surveyed, respondents mostly (45%-63%) thought it was not too late to avert the worst impacts of the climate crisis but that it would require a drastic change in approach. Only 11%-24% believed it was already too late.
after newsletter promotion

Between 9% and 20% said they thought current measures would be enough to prevent the most serious impacts. But in terms of what climate actions had support, those not directly affecting people’s lives were the most popular.

Measures such as planting more trees, subsidising energy efficiency, banning single-use plastics and taxing big emitters were all favoured, while increasing fuel duty, limiting meat and dairy, taxing air fares and banning new petrol and diesel cars were opposed.

A similar pattern emerged when respondents were asked what steps they would be prepared to take: cheap and easy actions such as creating green space at home and eating only seasonal fruit and vegetables were popular, but not shopping exclusively secondhand or paying more for flights.

articles.title: Tanzania: Opposition leader Tundu Lissu jailed for four years
articles.summary: Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu has been sentenced to four years in prison after being cleared of treason. Lissu condemned his conviction for incitement, which had not been among the charges…

image.caption: Lissu had already spent 19 months in jail before receiving his four-year sentence (FILE: 19/05/2025)Image: Ericky Boniphase/DW

blocks.text: Tundu Lissu, the leader of Tanzania's main opposition party, was sentenced to four years in prison on Friday for incitement to unrest after being cleared of treason.
While the verdict removed the threat of a death sentence, judges convicted Lissu of an offense that was not among the charges he faced.
What did the court decide?
Judges found that Chadema leader Lissu's statements about blocking the election were intended to disrupt the vote and encourage violence.
"We are satisfied that through his statements, the accused intended to disrupt elections and instigate violence," the judge said.
Lissu disputed his conviction on a charge different from the treason accusation he had faced.
"I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles," he said, apparently referring to President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

Lissu was arrested in April 2025 over a speech in which prosecutors said he told supporters the opposition would "block the election" and "mobilize rebellion." He pleaded not guilty, arguing that his speech broke no law and that the prosecution was politically motivated. Lissu has already spent 19 months in jail.
The Tanzania voter boycott over opposition party exclusion
"All this was political persecution. Excuses were created to imprison me," he told the court after the verdict.
How did the case fuel Tanzania's unrest?
Lissu's arrest, alleged abductions of government critics, and Chadema's exclusion from the October 2025 election helped drive protests across the country.
Hundreds died as police opened fire on protesters in several cities. Opposition figures and rights groups put the toll in the thousands.

A commission appointed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan reported in April that at least 518 people had been killed and blamed protesters for the violence. The government denied allegations that security forces used excessive force.
Security was tightened in the commercial capital, Dar es Salaam, and around the courthouse ahead of Friday's verdict.
Why has the trial drawn international criticism?
British and European Union lawmakers described the case as politically motivated and called for Lissu's immediate release.
"The use of capital punishment against a political opponent risks turning the justice system into an instrument of political repression," they wrote to Hassan.
Meet Tundu Lissu: The leader of Tanzania's Chadema party
Lissu, 58, has been repeatedly arrested for opposing the government. In 2017, he survived an assassination attempt in which he was shot 16 times. He believes the attack was politically motivated.

articles.title: "No choice but to bear it": Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
articles.summary: Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a…

image.caption: Experts say restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels [FILE: November 9, 2025]Image: Arvind Yadav/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.

"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."
Not too long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.

Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of pollution.
"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.
A recurring crisis

Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.

On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.

Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.
But despite years of attempted interventions, India's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.

blocks.caption: The issue has persisted for years despite public outrage [FILE: November 6, 2025]Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is causing the air pollution?
Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.

A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.

"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.
Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.
"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.
Why aren't anti-pollution policies working?
To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements, Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.
"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.

According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.

blocks.caption: Delhi has imposed restrictions on vehicles under a certain emission standard [FILE: December 19, 2025]Image: Sunil Ghosh/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."
Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.

"They allow pollution to occur and then try to clean it up — producing nice photo opportunities of water sprinklers and smog guns, or talking about cloud seeding," Kandhari told DW. "Creating pollution only to clean it up later is a waste of public funds, time, and health."
Kandhari also added that incinerating waste instead of proper waste management has only exacerbated the situation.
The politics of pollution
Another obstacle to a lasting solution has been the political blame game that starts as soon as the air quality worsens.

On Thursday, Delhi Environment Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa said stubble-burning in the neighboring state of Punjab is contributing to the capital's rising pollution, according to public broadcaster All India Radio. He insisted that in Delhi, construction, vehicle and industrial sources were controlled.

Dahiya agreed that seasonal crop-burning fires in neighboring states of Punjab and Haryana "is an episodic but sharp contributor" which "can tip 'very poor' air into 'severe'" for a few weeks. But it is not the lone contributor.

"Among sources within Delhi, vehicles alone contribute roughly 51-53% of local PM2.5. A large share of winter PM2.5 is also secondary particulate formed from gases like sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and ammonia," Dahiya said. "That points straight back to combustion in power plants, industry and transport."
"If stubble burning ended tomorrow, Delhi would still breathe unhealthy air for most of the year," he added.
DW reached out to several Delhi government officials for a response, but received no reply.
What needs to change?
Delhi is also home to millions of people who cannot afford air purifiers and have no escape from the toxic air.
Among them is Deepika, who works as domestic help in an affluent South Delhi neighborhood. She has been coughing for a week.
It is the same every year, she said.
"I have no choice but to bear it for the next few months."

blocks.caption: Water sprinklers and smog towers provide some relief but experts say deeper reform is needed [FILE: December 16, 2025]Image: Arun Sankar/AFP

blocks.text: The people DW spoke to point to a common set of priorities: Addressing Delhi's pollution crisis requires year-round pollution control rather than seasonal restrictions, better coordination between governments and stronger enforcement of existing regulations and measurable targets. They say the city needs a sustained clean-air strategy more than another winter emergency plan.
Namrata Yadav is a Delhi resident and the mother of an eight-year-old boy. They both joined protests against air pollution in November. A year later, the problems persist.
"It is exhausting to repeat the same things year after year, only to be dismissed as paranoid or alarmist for demanding something as basic as clean air," she said.

Calling for lasting solutions driven by science, policy and accountability, Yadav said: "We have spent years learning how to live with pollution. It is time we demanded that those responsible learn how to end it."
Smog chokes New Delhi despite India's push against pollution

articles.title: Kenya cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years
articles.summary: A court in Kenya has sentenced Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and an adult. He told them to starve themselves to death as part of his apocalyptic religious cult.

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie was convicted earlier this year, and could potentially have faced the death sentence Image: Luis Tato/AFP

blocks.text: Kenyan religious sect leader Paul Mackenzie was sentenced to 200 years in prison on Friday, at the culmination of a trial following the discovery of hundreds of corpses in the woods.

A self-proclaimed pastor and longstanding leader of a new age Christian apocalyptic cult called the Good News International Church, Mackenzie was convicted in October of 191 counts of murder in the deaths of one adult and 190 children.
Justice Diana Kavedza said the sentence was comprised of 100 years for 183 counts of murder by starvation and another 100 years for eight counts of murder by direct homicide.
He could have faced the death penalty, which is still technically on the books in Kenya.
However, like several countries that have kept capital punishment in their legal code but stopped actually using it, Kenya has not executed anybody since 1987.

While the charges against Mackenzie pertained to 191 deaths, some 400 people were found dead in what became known as the "Shakahola Forest Massacre." Mackenzie's so-called church had been operating since 2003, based in the coastal town of Malindi.
Mackenzie had denied the charges, saying that he did not force the cult followers to starve.
A total of 28 accomplices were given various prison sentences for their roles in the deaths.

articles.title: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
articles.summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".

blocks.text: A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to life in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 27 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
Ahead of sentencing, prosecutors in the court in Mombasa had argued for the death penalty for Mackenzie because of the gravity of the crimes.
The prosecutors also cited what they described as Mackenzie's lack of remorse for the crimes. They requested life sentences for his co-accused.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives in Shakahola forest, including two grandchildren, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused have formally pleaded for mercy and asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Diana Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.
Those who opposed Mackenzie's teachings were beaten to death.
One of his co-accused said he had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows".
Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings" and those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus" the judge said.
The judge found that the deaths arose from an organised system, including religious teachings and directives that compelled followers to follow the deadly fasting.
Post-mortem results showed the cause of deaths to be starvation for most victims, while others died from suffocation, strangulation or head injuries.
The cause of death could not be determined for some, with their bodies having decomposed, while others died soon after their rescue as they were so emaciated.
The Shakahola deaths have shone a spotlight on the lack of oversight of rogue religious activities and how they could have carried on for so long.
The gravity of the case prompted President William Ruto to set up a commission of inquiry, although this was later declared unconstitutional.

Investigations by the state-funded Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) revealed that local administration and law enforcement officials had repeatedly turned a blind eye to the cult's activities.
"We expected at that time the police would take action immediately to go and rescue the other members there, but it didn't happen", says Wanje, who reported the case to the police in March 2023.

Wanje says a relative of his in the police force and a former cult participant managed to save his grandson at the time. The child told the police what had happened and showed them the grave of his siblings.
"It was his last day.. they [would have killed] my grandson."
The cult leader had previously been arrested and later released for lack of evidence.
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003.
Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity, drawing thousands of followers in its branches across Kenya.
The church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

While the conclusion of the murder cases may bring a sense of justice for the victims and their families, the convictions only account for 191 victims, while more than 400 bodies were exhumed from the forest.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.
