articles.title: Democratic socialist defeats incumbent Karen Bass in Los Angeles mayor's race
articles.summary: The results mean America's two most populous cities - New York and Los Angeles - will be led by democratic socialists.

blocks.text: Democratic socialist Nithya Raman has toppled incumbent Karen Bass in the race for mayor of Los Angeles.

Raman's win stunned political watchers in California after she entered the race as a long-shot candidate against Bass, a political heavyweight who previously served in Congress and had never lost a race for political office.
Raman has frequently been compared to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Both are democratic socialists and ran on progressive platforms.

Her win solidifies that America's two biggest cities will now be led by democratic socialists, which include some of the most high-profile politicians in the US, such as Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
Los Angeles was always likely to have a Democratic mayor but the question in the city - the second most populous city in the US - was just how left voters would be willing to go.

Bass, also Democrat, announced that she had called and conceded to Raman in a post on social media on Thursday, writing "while this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken."

"Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote. "I love Los Angeles. I believe in Los Angeles. And I will continue to ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."

items: Boebert, billionaires' tax and other midterms races still to watch
Food, fuel and taxes – can the Democrats actually make life cheaper?
'This is a disaster': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat

blocks.text: Raman, a member of city council and Indian immigrant, ran on a platform of change and fixing the "broken status quo and the politicians who failed them over and over again".

She ran on cutting homelessness, increasing housing in the city, saving Hollywood jobs from continued cuts and protecting residents from immigration enforcement efforts. Raman also vowed to fix the city's many issues, including helping beautification efforts, fixing roads and even helping bring back nightlife in the city.

The major issue in the race, however, was the LA fires, which killed dozens of people and razed neighbourhoods across the area in 2025. Bass faced intense political fallout over her absence during the emergency and the city's response to the disaster.
The next mayor in LA will oversee hosting the Super Bowl in 2027 and the 2028 Summer Olympics.

articles.title: Delhi's toxic winter air is back - is the Indian capital prepared for pollution?
articles.summary: The Delhi government has announced a four-month winter action plan, but experts say that won't be enough.

blocks.text: There are two cardboard boxes in Meenu Rana's living room in Delhi. One is filled with Diwali decorations and twinkling lights. The other holds air purifiers.
"The mornings have already started feeling stuffy. It will get worse in the coming days, so it's better to be prepared," says the 43-year-old teacher.
She is not alone. Every year, as winter and the festive season approach, residents of India's capital begin preparing for something far less celebratory: months of breathing polluted air.
Delhi and its satellite cities record some of the world's highest pollution levels through the year. But as winter sets in, the air often becomes unbearable.

Falling temperatures and slower winds trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. Smoke from crop residue burning in neighbouring states adds to emissions from vehicles and factories, as well as construction dust. Firecrackers used during festivals often worsen air quality.
The result is noxious air and a familiar question: why does pollution return year after year, and why hasn't more been done to tackle it?

This year, however, the Delhi government announced its Winter Action Plan months before the worst of the smog arrived. The plan is in place from 1 November to 28 February, covering the months when pollution usually spikes.

Experts have called this a step in the right direction, noting that in previous years measures were often rolled out only after the air quality got too bad to ignore. However, they say this by itself won't be enough, calling for more holistic, long-lasting measures.
Just days after the plan came into effect, the city is slipping back into a depressingly familiar pattern.

This week, a grey haze hangs over Delhi, along with a distinct smoky smell that residents unwillingly recognise. People complain of irritation in their eyes and difficulty breathing, and coughs and sneezes are heard everywhere.

For those who can afford them, air purifiers have become a household necessity. Outdoors, people wear masks or cover their faces with cloth, trying to protect themselves from the worst of the pollution.
Tackling pollution was among the promises made by the governing Bharatiya Janata Party during its election campaign last year. Its winter action plan is now a major test of that pledge.

The plan restricts the entry of older, more polluting vehicles registered outside Delhi and denies fuel to vehicles without a certificate which shows they meet emission standards. Demolitions and outdoor construction work that generate dust have been temporarily banned.

Private vehicle use is being discouraged - the government has asked offices to allow half of their employees to work from home, introduced staggered office timings for its staff and doubled parking charges. It says it will also strengthen pollution monitoring and enforcement and promote public transport and electric vehicles.
These measures are separate from the Graded Response Action Plan (Grap), which is overseen by the federal Commission for Air Quality Management.

Grap introduces restrictions in stages, with stricter measures kicking in as pollution levels rise. This week, its second stage is in force, restricting the use of diesel generators and burning of coal and firewood.
Expert say on paper, these actions collectively provide a roadmap for responding to rising pollution levels but their success ultimately depends on enforcement.

"There are a lot of positive changes as far as planning is concerned, but when it comes to execution, we probably still stand at the same level," says Parthaa Bosu, strategic adviser at the Environmental Defense Fund, a non-profit group focused on delivering climate solutions.
Others argue that the problem goes much deeper.

"If we want to reduce pollution, we need to set targets for every sector - including power generation, industry and transport - not just vehicle entry, construction and stubble burning," says Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
"We know how much each sector and each state contributes to pollution. We can set targets to reduce emissions from each of them over the next five years."

Bosu points out that an issue which does not get enough attention is secondary pollutants - when gases in the air react with sunlight, water vapour and other substances to form harmful particles that contribute to pollution.

"Pollution is not just caused by biomass burning or vehicles," he says. "Dust being stirred up from the ground, coal and fly ash, materials burned at brick kilns and the large-scale burning of urban waste are also contributing to the problem. And much of this is still not being stopped."

Delhi's pollution problem is also affected by what happens outside the city. Pollutants travel into Delhi from neighbouring states and other parts of northern India, worsening the situation, Bosu explains.
This means that measures taken by Delhi can achieve only so much. Tackling the problem requires neighbouring states and the wider northern region to work together, he adds.

items: 'I panic every time she coughs' - Delhi's toxic air is making its children sick
Why India caps pollution reading at 500 when the air is far more toxic
Can artificial rain fix toxic air in India's capital?
Living in Delhi smog is like watching a dystopian film again and again

blocks.text: In the meantime, pollution is harming people's health every day.
During winter, government monitoring stations in Delhi frequently record Air Quality Index (AQI) readings above 300, classified as "very poor".

On particularly bad days, readings can reach 500, the highest point on India's scale. That does not mean pollution cannot rise further, only that domestic trackers do not record it. International trackers such as Swiss-based IQAir have recorded readings close to 1,000 on some days.

The World Health Organization recommends average PM2.5 levels over 24 hours should not exceed 15 micrograms per cubic metre. In Delhi, levels are often at more than 25 times that limit during pollution season.

Dr Manoj Goel, pulmonology unit head at Fortis Memorial Research Institute near Delhi, says these tiny particles "can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, triggering inflammation and affecting multiple organs".
Even short-term exposure can cause throat irritation, coughing, wheezing and breathlessness. It can also worsen existing heart and lung conditions.
A 2025 report, external by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago estimated that air pollution could reduce life expectancy in Delhi by up to 8.2 years.
For residents, the challenge is not just limited to breathing. The restrictions also disrupt everyday life.

Delhi is closely connected to its satellite towns, Noida and Gurugram, with thousands of people travelling between them every day for work. Long queues form at the city's borders as vehicles are stopped and checked, leaving commuters stuck in traffic for hours.
While the new rules offer some hope, frustration is growing.
Protests, political arguments and court interventions have become part of the annual cycle. But despite public pressure and government measures, the pollution returns every winter.
Rana keeps her windows closed and curtains drawn, and has added more indoor plants.
The arrival of another winter fills her family with dread, but unlike many others, they are not planning to move out of Delhi.
"I would have left the city long ago had there been an option, but my son has his school, my husband and I have our jobs as well, which makes it practically impossible," she says.
"What option do we have? It is unfair but we will have to live with it."

articles.title: PR expert says author Steven Galloway had path to rehabilitate reputation
articles.summary: Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.

image.caption: Bestselling author Steven Galloway is seen in his former office at the University of British Columbia in March 2014. A public relations expert testified on Thursday in an ongoing defamation trial launched by Galloway. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Galloway, a former University of British Columbia writing professor, is suing multiple people who published allegations of sexual assault against him.
Author is suing his accuser and others over statements about him
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Nov 05, 2026 6:10 PM EST | Last Updated: 6 minutes ago

A public relations expert told British Columbia Supreme Court that author and former University of B.C. professor Steven Galloway could have done more to rehabilitate his reputation after he was accused of rape more than a decade ago.

Norman Stowe, a reputation rehabilitation, public relations and crisis management expert, testified on Thursday in the trial of Galloway's defamation lawsuit against his accuser and others who published unproven allegations against him.

"To be blunt, I've worked with clients who had far less going for them than Mr. Galloway in terms of the capacity to go out and defend your reputation or rehabilitate your reputation," said Stowe, a managing partner of the public affairs company Pace Group.

Stowe produced a report for the defence of Galloway's accuser, a woman known as A.B., whose name is subject to a publication ban. He told the court that while he had never worked on a file involving a rape accusation, efforts to rehabilitate someone's reputation involve the same steps regardless of the nature of the issue.
Former UBC professor Steven Galloway’s defamation trial begins

The trial heard Stowe's report included examples of other high-profile people who suffered reputational damage, such as Bill Clinton, Martha Stewart and Tiger Woods, but he agreed under cross-examination that allegations against them were not in the same "universe" as a rape accusation.
A.B.'s defence does not allege she was sexually assaulted, rather that she reported the alleged assaults.
Galloway denies the assault claims, and alleges they destroyed his career.

items: Steven Galloway testifies that faculty-student relationships in UBC arts program were common
'Outrageous' rhetoric alleged in emails as Steven Galloway defamation trial continues

blocks.text: The court previously heard from a publishing industry expert who said the author of the hit novel The Cellist of Sarajevo had potentially lost millions of dollars in future income.

Stowe said some of Pace Group's high-profile clients have included the Vancouver Airport Authority following the death of Robert Dziekanski — who died after being Tasered by Mounties at the airport in 2007 — and B.C. Ferries after the sinking of the Queen of the North.
"We have also worked on several cases that involve sexual activities. I can't say much more than that," he said.
Multiple people apologized
The court heard Stowe believed Galloway had a "strong path to reputational rehabilitation" and could have resumed some version of his writing career.
But he conceded under questioning by Galloway's lawyer, Daniel Burnett, that his report incorrectly stated the author had made no efforts to do so.
Burnett said Stewart, Clinton and Woods were all "guilty" of what they'd been accused of, and asked Stowe about a different approach to restoring the reputation of someone who is innocent.

Stowe said he didn't have access to some documents in Galloway's case, including the full report by a retired judge, Mary Ellen Boyd, who found the assault allegations against the author unsubstantiated.

Stowe told the court Boyd's report could have been used as leverage in rehabilitating Galloway's reputation, along with support from those in the literary community who had publicly called for due process for the author.
Bestselling author Steven Galloway's defamation trial in 4th week
But Stowe said "there was no plan, no linking these things together to help him get past this and rehabilitate so he could reclaim some part of his personal life and professional life."
Stowe believed Galloway had many opportunities "to bring all these things together, but that never seemed to materialize," he said.
He said he thought the author had "sort of given up," thinking "his life was over."

He agreed that rape allegations are "powerful." But he said Galloway's attempts to refute the claims against him were not part of a plan to rehabilitate his reputation, and the efforts "sort of started and then stalled."

items: UBC prof testifies she acted as a 'conduit' for sex assault allegations against Steven Galloway
Sex assault allegations diminished performance of Steven Galloway's books: industry expert

blocks.text: Stowe said he didn't review social media posts about Galloway, which Burnett said came in "waves … over years and years" leading to the defamation lawsuit.
Stowe's testimony concluded Thursday and defendant Mandi Gray was next to take the stand.
Galloway alleges Gray, an assistant professor at Trent University in Ontario, defamed him in a series of social media posts.
Several people originally named as defendants in Galloway's lawsuit, filed in 2018, have settled with him and offered public apologies.

articles.title: Man accused of killing 11-year-old Burnaby boy makes 1st court appearance
articles.summary: One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.

image.caption: Branko Bijelic appears by video link in B.C. Provincial Court in Vancouver on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (CBC News)

blocks.text: British Columbia
One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.
Branko Bijelic is charged with 2nd-degree murder in the death of Kai Pavlovic
One of two people charged in relation to the death of an 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy appeared in a Vancouver courtroom for the first time on Thursday.
Branko Bijelic, 51, is charged with second-degree murder and indignity to human remains in the death of Kai Pavlovic.
He and 46-year-old Sarah Bijelic, who was also charged with manslaughter in the case, were both family members of the boy, according to police.
A publication ban prevents CBC News from reporting on any details about Sarah Bijelic's court proceedings.
Police allege Kai Pavlovic was killed prior to being reported missing on Sept. 26, 2025. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
Branko, who has yet to enter a plea, appeared by video link dressed in a red sweatshirt and glasses.
He sat quietly during proceedings, which were put over until later this month.

items: Family members charged in homicide of missing 11-year-old Burnaby, B.C., boy

blocks.text: A family member from New Zealand, who identified herself as Kai's grandmother, was present in court gallery, but declined to speak with journalists.
In a statement to CBC News, Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains "absolutely devastated" by his death, and will "forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts."
Kai's aunt Helen Kok said the family remains 'absolutely devastated' by his death, and will 'forever have a Kai shaped hole in our hearts.' (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
"Kai was the light of our lives and we will miss the joy, creativity, and sense of adventure he brought with him wherever he went — and that is how we will remember him," the statement adds.
"We are grateful for closure after a long time of not knowing."
The family also asked the public to refrain from judgement, conjecture and speculation.

items: Burnaby RCMP renew call for information as search continues for missing 11-year-old boy

blocks.text: The Lower Mainland's Integrated Homicide Investigation Team (IHIT) announced charges in the case on Nov. 2, more than a year after the boy was reported missing.
Police allege Kai was killed prior to being reported missing on Sept. 26, 2025.
The boy's remains were discovered at an undisclosed location earlier this year, according to IHIT. (Submitted by Burnaby RCMP)
According to police, Burnaby RCMP had received a request to check on the boy's well-being that day, and escalated the case to the Serious Crimes Unit when they were unable to locate him.
The case was later escalated again to IHIT.

items: Mounties in Burnaby, B.C., searching for missing 11-year-old boy

blocks.text: The boy's remains were discovered at an undisclosed location earlier this year, according to IHIT.
Family members have launched a fundraiser with the goal of transporting Kai's remains to Montenegro so he can be buried with his father, and for the creation of a memorial garden in New Zealand.
With files from Michelle Ghoussoub and Amelia John

articles.title: Will Atiku Abubakar be on Nigeria's presidential ballot after court ruling?
articles.summary: The high court has sacked the leadership of the opposition ADC party with only months to go until elections.

blocks.text: Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"

In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
The ADC is seen as the most powerful opposition to President Tinubu. Many influential politicians opposed to the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have already defected to the party.
The legal saga could complicate things - it may cause uncertainty for hundreds of ADC candidates as well as raise questions over who has the authority to represent them.
But Abubakar, who is running for the presidency for a seventh time, is confident the matter will be resolved and called on his supporters not to be distracted.

"Nigerians deserve relief from this crushing cost-of-living crisis. We urge our supporters to remain resolute, take our message from house to house and door to door, and stay peaceful and focused," the 79-year-old said.
Peter Obi - the other main presidential candidate, who is on the ballot for a second time - has said he is shocked by Thursday's high court ruling.
He released a statement on X with the heading, external: "Do not undermine democracy".
The 65-year-old went on to say: "My concern is that three months before a general election, it is in the public interest to have certainty.
Obi had briefly joined the ADC before leaving earlier this year to join the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) - in part because of the legal challenges within the ADC.

"The sustenance of democracy in Nigeria, in the midst of encroaching military rule in West Africa, should strengthen our resolve to protect opposition politics and not stamp out opposition parties," he said.
The NDC's candidate said that, as president, he would ensure that the existence of opposition parties would be respected.
"This is a time to strengthen our democracy by allowing the opposition to thrive."
Additional reporting by Chris Ewokor in Abuja

articles.title: From gas to groceries, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?
articles.summary: The 2026 budget increases payments for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and expands a tax credit for low-wage workers. But the affordability measures are mostly for the short term, and…

image.caption: Loblaws customers shop at a Toronto-area grocery store on March 6, 2025. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

The 2026 budget increases payments for the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and expands a tax credit for low-wage workers. But the affordability measures are mostly for the short term, and took a back seat to measures aimed at boosting investment.
Push to spur investment overshadows affordability moves: economist
From a grocery benefit expansion to rental assistance and payments for more low-wage workers, Thursday's federal budget includes a number of measures aimed at making life more affordable.
But they were still eclipsed by a focus on investment.
One of the main direct pocketbook measures is a top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — a pre-existing program that gives quarterly payments to Canadians with low and modest incomes.

The top-up will increase those payments by 50 per cent for the 2026-27 program year. Combined with previous increases, a single person could get up to $1,290. A couple with two children could get up to $2,570.

items: Carney's 2nd budget earmarks billions for affordability and Canadian sovereignty
Budget 2026: Ottawa bets on investment, major projects to boost Canada's economy

blocks.text: The government says the program will give Canadians collectively $4.1 billion more in support to help pay for essentials.

More low-income workers will also get benefit payments to help them make ends meet. Those who make a minimum of $3,000 annually get a refundable tax credit under the Canada Workers Benefit, but that threshold is being lowered to $500 for all workers. The budget also increases those credits slightly, to $1,859 for single individuals who don't have kids and $3,143 for families.

Other measures aimed at bringing down costs were already announced. The government suspended the excise tax on fuel — which saves Canadians about 10 cents a litre on the cost of gasoline — in April, and later extended that to the end of January 2027. The tax will come back at a 50 per cent rate until the end of March 2027 and then return to its regular level.
In all, the budget shows the government spending $5.3 billion on that relief at the pumps.
Here’s why you’re paying more for diesel
Overall, the federal government's fiscal plan pledges $22 billion for new spending on affordability measures.

But aside from that direct spending on things like groceries and gas — measures that will support Canadians in the short term — economist Armine Yalnizyan says there's little in the budget for everyday people.
"It's not like they're doing nothing," Yalnizyan said. "But the short answer is Canadians are going to need a lot of patience because this budget is not there to support them."

The biggest-ticket spending on affordability is related to housing, with $11.2 billion dedicated to ending homelessness within 10 years. That money would help build supportive and transitional housing and provide support to facilities that care for people in a mental health or substance abuse crisis.

To help low-income renters, the government is also renewing the Canada Housing Benefit for 10 years to support Canadians with direct monthly rental assistance, to the tune of $1.7 billion starting in the 2028-29 fiscal year.

Yalnizyan said the pledge to end homelessness is a welcome one — as is the commitment to extend the ban on foreign purchases of rental properties to January 2026. But the housing benefit doesn't go far enough, she says, and the money to fund new housing projects won't benefit Canadians for years to come.

New homes under construction in the community of Upper Caledon East. The federal budget pledged $11.2 billion to end homelessness, as well as more money to build non-market housing and regular homes. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)
"There is money there for it but it's not coming through fast enough," Yalnizyan said. "There's too much wait and see, come and talk to us later," Yalnizyan said.

Those affordability measures are also eclipsed by tax cuts and investments in infrastructure and other major projects. The previously announced productivity mega-deduction alone accounts for $36 billion worth of spending, compared to $22 billion overall for affordability.
Rather than boosting everyday Canadians, Yalnizyan says the budget is focused on catalyzing investment and attracting new spending within Canada.
"It's not a bad budget for all of that, but they've left out the people," Yalnizyan said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Abby Hughes is a writer with CBC News based in Toronto. Originally from Orillia, Ont., she studied journalism at Toronto Metropolitan University. She covers news from the worlds of business, entertainment, health, science and education, and her favourite stories focus on the real people in those areas — the customers, fans, patients, citizens and students. You can reach her with story ideas at abby.hughes@cbc.ca.
With files from Nisha Patel

articles.title: California governor commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
articles.summary: California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates in the US.

blocks.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead with life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.

The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been killed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.

Newsom, describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".

He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
The decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US.

On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.

articles.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after review, sexual assault allegations
articles.summary: Months after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on the set of Married at First Sight UK, the results of an external review have prompted Channel 4 to decide not…

image.caption: Married at First Sight UK will not return to Channel 4, and the show's budget will be reinvested in new programming, following the results of an external review of contributor welfare. (Channel 4)

blocks.text: Entertainment

Months after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on the set of Married at First Sight UK, the results of an external review have prompted Channel 4 to decide not to bring the show back.
Channel 4 says show will not return after 3 female contestants alleged misconduct
Britain's Channel 4 says it will not bring back Married at First Sight UK, following the results of an external review into contributor welfare.
It was commissioned after three female cast members came forward with allegations of sexual assault on set.
The show follows strangers matched by relationship experts who meet for the first time at the altar, take part in a mock wedding ceremony and move in together as newlyweds.
The U.K. version of the program was considered to be a massive ratings juggernaut for Channel 4, and ran for 10 seasons.

In May, BBC's current affairs program Panorama spoke to two women who said they were raped by their on-screen husbands, and a third who alleged her on-screen husband subjected her to a non-consensual sexual act.

items: Married at First Sight UK pulls episodes after brides allege sexual assault by co-stars

blocks.text: The men denied the allegations. In June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.
Channel 4 commissioned a review tasked with examining whether the show's welfare protocols met its duty of care obligations — and whether those protocols needed to be changed.
The results of that review, released Thursday, found the show's welfare protocols were extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard — though in some isolated incidents, not fully implemented.
Measures to improve welfare

The final report also included recommendations to improve the welfare of Married at First Sight UK cast members — including putting couples in separate bedrooms on wedding night and honeymoon, reviewing the frequency with which couples are asked about the physical side of their relationship, and removing Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.

It also suggested installing CCTV and sound recording equipment in all areas of the apartments to be monitored 24/7 by a welfare-trained team, and providing two lockable ensuite bedrooms for cast members.
Channel 4 headquarters in London, U.K. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)

"MAFS UK has been enjoyed by millions of viewers, made possible by the willingness of its contributors to embrace the social experiment at the heart of the show and the many talented people involved in its production," said Channel 4 chief executive Priya Dogra in a statement.
She thanked the team for its efforts to protect the welfare of contributors, but said "the series will not return to Channel 4, with the show’s budget reinvested in distinctive new programming."
Dogra also repeated her apology to the female cast members who came forward with their allegations.

"This review did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama program, but I would like to repeat that I am very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt."
She said she hopes Channel 4's swift action demonstrates "our desire to relentlessly strengthen industry standards."
The show is part of an international reality-TV franchise with editions in countries including the U.S. and Australia.
CBC News has not had any response to questions about whether those shows will continue.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Melania Trump calls for lasting Ukraine truce as she hosts Russian and Ukrainian officials
articles.summary: The US first lady was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire.

blocks.text: US First Lady Melania Trump called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine as she welcomed Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House following last week's truce in the southern region of Kherson.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire, which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.
"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.
The unusual White House event saw senior Ukrainian and Russian officials meet away from the setting of official US-brokered peace talks they have been holding without success since last year.

The delegations were made up of Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
Melania Trump was credited by all for playing a key though unspecified role in the ceasefire, and all parties conveyed to her the gratitude of the Russian and Ukrainian presidents.
The US first lady said she had "reviewed demining plans, aerial images, assessed roadways, and discussed evacuation routes, hospital access, vehicles, and medical resources" during the truce.

"Last week in Oleshky and neighbouring areas of Kherson, people experienced the simple joys of life for the first time since 2022," Trump said. "They walked down familiar streets without fear of explosions."

She thanked both Volodymyr Zelensky and Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when the Russian president launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.
Dmitriev, a businessman and Kremlin special envoy who has previously represented Moscow during peace talks with Ukraine, thanked Trump for "saving and touching so many lives".
"Let us continue making a humanitarian contribution together; this is within our power," Dmitriev said, before gifting Melania Trump a framed drawing by an 11-year-old Oleshky evacuee.
He also praised Trump for her work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war. These include children allegedly abducted by Russia.

Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament who has also been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team, said the Oleshky ceasefire had constituted the "biggest de-escalation since 2022".
"We are creating a momentum where both sides are learning the… mechanics of how to actually keep the peace when the peace comes," he added.
He acknowledged that the "political track" of negotiations to end the conflict was "complex" but said Ukrainians were asking Melania Trump "to keep going and find new missions and de-escalate more."
At the end of the event, Trump handed Dmitriev and Arakhamia two letters to be hand-delivered to their respective presidents.
The White House later said Melania Trump had invited her guests to view two historic artifacts which she had "personally selected as powerful symbols of peace".

One was an 18th Century medicine chest which was removed from the White House when the British set it on fire in 1812. "Once adversaries, the United States and Great Britain ultimately established a strong alliance," the White House said.
The second artifact was a cup gifted in 1899 to the French ambassador in recognition of his efforts to bring the Spanish-American war to an end.

Melania Trump has generally remained discreet on foreign policy matters, and neither Moscow nor Kyiv have elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement in coordinating the delicate ceasefire - the most enduring and widespread of the war so far.
A source who works in the local government of the Kherson region told the BBC that work on the Oleshky evacuation had been ongoing for almost a year.

However, the source said, "at a certain point other individuals became involved, seemingly after most of the groundwork had already been laid and subsequently began taking credit for the progress that had been made."

It was difficult to determine exactly who had played what role and at which stage of the process, the source acknowledged, adding that "those who had been directly involved in the negotiations for nearly a year were eventually prohibited from communicating publicly about the matter."

Speaking after the meeting in the White House had taken place, President Zelensky said the success of the Oleshky ceasefire "had proved a very simple thing: when Putin wants the fighting to stop, it stops."
"The same applies to our people who are held in Russian captivity. When Putin wants, they go home."

A source close to American officials shared a similar assessment, implying to the BBC that despite the outward praise, "the person who made [the ceasefire] possible, whether we like it or not, is essentially Putin."
"And this was done in order to pass the ball to [Donald] Trump... so that it would have some positive effect for his midterm elections."
There has been no change whatsoever in Russia's position, Ukrainian political analyst Dmytro Levus told the BBC.

Moscow "agreed to it because there was pressure from the American side... In doing so, the Russians confirmed Zelenskyy's words that, when necessary, it turns out Russia can quickly stop firing and even maintain that ceasefire."
As the frontline region of Kherson experienced its first six days of peace in several years, the rest of Ukraine continued to come under Russian attack.

This week, several drone and missile attacks killed and injured civilians across the country. On Monday alone, more than 40 people were killed in a single Russian strike on an aid distribution centre in the region of Zaporizhzhia. More are thought to still be buried under the rubble.
Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko in Kyiv

articles.title: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we meet a group of youth who are helping people understand the impact of climate change on brain health; find out just how super this year's El Niño is…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it’s Bridget! When I heard there was an internship where Canadian youth were learning about how climate change and brain health are connected, while also creating accessible resources to teach others, I knew I had to find out more.
This week:

items: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain
The Big Picture: The Super El Niño
Hungry animals and local farmers want your leftover Halloween pumpkins

blocks.text: Canadian youth are helping others understand how climate change affects the brain

A screenshot from a virtual showcase held on Oct. 18, where students from around the country presented the neuroscience research projects they had been working on this summer. (Brain Climate Equity Collaborative)

Doctors know that climate impacts such as wildfire smoke and extreme heat lead to physical ailments like asthma and heat exhaustion. But more research has been coming out about how climate-related events are also harming the brain, and are linked to anxiety and higher rates of dementia and cognitive functioning issues.

Neuroscience graduate student Muskaan Laroyia researches how climate change affects neurological conditions — something she has discussed at length with others in the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine.
“There was a huge gap between how we perceive brain health, and the impact that the climate crisis is having on brain health,” said Laroyia.
Laroyia co-founded the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative to empower young people to do something about it, as they are most affected by eco-anxiety.

“Recent research has said that the best way to approach eco-anxiety, especially in youth, is not just to tell them all the negative things that are happening but to help them be a part of that change,” she said.

One of the ways Laroyia and her colleagues are addressing this is through their NeuroClimate Youth Internship, launched this year with the University of Calgary’s O'Brien Institute for Public Health. The goal is to help youth learn more about the link between climate change and brain health, and then help them turn that knowledge into action.
Safina Pamery’s group worked over the summer to create accessible resources about the impacts of climate on brain health. (Submitted by Safina Pamery)

From July to October, 30 high school students from across the country worked with researchers and clinicians to explore the intersections of climate change, brain health and health equity. The students attended expert lectures, including a talk from a neuroscientist from Stanford, and a panel with the creators of the University of Toronto’s MedComic Con talking about different ways to disseminate information creatively.
By the end of the internship, the students had produced accessible digital resources for health-care professionals and the public highlighting climate impacts on the brain and what to do about them.
They created websites, presentations and short stories covering everything from how wildfire smoke and air quality affect the brain to how to recognize eco-anxiety and respond to it in healthy ways.
The internship culminated in a virtual international showcase on Oct. 18, where the students presented their research projects and answered questions from researchers, clinicians and other attendees.
Khushi Laroyia led her group’s work on extreme heat and the neurological effects it can have. (Submitted by Khushi Laroyia)

Coincidentally, Laroyia's younger sister, Khushi Laroyia, was among the students chosen by an independent committee to participate in the program. Khushi Laroyia says she learned a lot about how much climate change can impact health equity in vulnerable communities, such as older adults, people with mental health conditions, and those without access to air conditioning and cool spaces.
“Before this internship, I never thought about how climate change doesn't just affect the environment — it affects people, it affects their brain, it affects their mental health,” she said.
“It really opened my eyes to things that I wouldn't ordinarily think about.”
Her group created a website with interactive guides, case studies and toolkits with resources to help people cope with eco-anxiety and figure out how to take action.
Making information accessible

Samarth Yandhe, 15, participated in the internship from Mississauga. Yandhe interviewed people in his community to find real-life examples of how people are struggling with smoke and was surprised to learn that people were not very informed about microscopic particles called PM2.5 that can affect brain function.
He turned research and statistics into short text blurbs that anyone could understand with no prior knowledge of the science.
Samarth Yandhe, 15, is one of the youngest internship participants. He now hopes to study neuroscience at university. (Submitted by Samarth Yandhe)
“Learning about this in more detail made me think about how I spend my day,” said Yandhe, who says the project has made him think differently about things like water usage and littering.

He now realizes that all environmental degradation can harm human health, including the brain, whereas actions to improve the environment, such as conserving water and picking up trash, can improve people's health.
“If I want to help our community and others, I have to start being the type of person who would change for others.”
This is exactly what the Brain Climate Equity Collaborative is meant to inspire — a new understanding of how climate and the brain are interconnected.
“Research is very siloed, it remains in journals, and what we're trying to do is bring that information out to the public,” said Daniela Oboh, the co-executive director of the Collaborative.
There are also plans underway for another internship cohort next year, and Laroyia and Oboh have already received interest from medical schools and community organizations.
And the students haven’t stopped at the presentations. They continue to share their work through ongoing community activities, lectures and articles.
“I'm so proud of these students,” said Oboh. “Our future is very, very bright.”
— Bridget Stringer-Holden

When I lived in Lesotho in Southern Africa my attic was filled with bats. Each evening around sunset I would watch as they flew away for their night time hunting. And speaking of extinction I highly recommend the novel Beasts of the Sea by Iida Turpeinen."

Gillian Arsenault and John Virag asked if vertical axis wind turbines, like some of the ones in our 2023 article on rooftop wind turbines (see animation below), might be safer for birds and bats. The Big Picture: The Super El Niño
(Climate Central)

At the beginning of the year, no one could have predicted just how strong an El Niño would develop. But by June, it became clear that not only would we be getting an El Niño, but it could be one for the record books.

In its June monthly update, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said that there was a chance that the El Niño “would rank among the largest El Niño events in the historical record going back to 1950.” And boy were they right.

Here’s what that really means: El Niño is part of a natural cycle where ocean temperatures in a particular region of the Pacific Ocean rise above average. Anything more than 2 C is considered a strong El Niño. Well, the temperature anomaly has risen to 3.5 C. That’s why some people are calling it a “super” El Niño.

As you can see above, the ocean temperature is a sweltering 30 C in the part of the central Pacific near the equator used to monitor El Niño events. And it hasn’t even peaked yet. That’s forecast to happen in either November or December. Why does this matter? It influences weather patterns around the world, with the largest impacts being droughts and heavy rainfall in regions mainly around the equator. For Canada, it means dry conditions in the already drought-stricken regions in the west and warmer temperatures across northern and central Canada. And an El Niño also helps to drive up the annual global temperature, which is already rising due to climate change.
— Nicole Mortillaro

blocks.text: Hungry animals and local farmers want your leftover Halloween pumpkins
Justine Beaumont and her pig, Cupcake, pose alongside the pile of leftover pumpkins that people have donated to Beaumont Acres after Halloween on Nov. 2. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Some southwestern Ontario farms and municipalities are encouraging residents to keep pumpkins out of the trash as the Halloween season comes to an end.
The Great Pumpkin Rescue is an Oxford County-based volunteer group that shares ways people can repurpose their pumpkins, including through recipes, donations and composting.

“There are, quite frankly, benefits to the community when you find a locale [that's] going to take them,” said volunteer Bryan Smith. “Southwestern Ontario will grow as farmers grow more food and sell that locally, which is good for us more broadly … because it’s stimulating the local economy.”
The initiative to repurpose pumpkins started more than a decade ago at Northlane Farm in Thamesford, Ont., which to this day collects pumpkins for its farming operations.
Now, the Great Pumpkin Rescue group compiles an annual list of area farms that will take pumpkins, squash and gourds during the first week of November.
“There are quite a number of extremely happy goats, pigs and chickens who just love to eat them,” Smith said. “We want them to be turned into something that feeds farm animals.”
Hungry hogs want your Halloween leftovers

Beaumont Acres, a sanctuary in London, Ont., has been accepting pumpkins from community members every fall since it opened six years ago. Founder Justine Beaumont estimates the farm has already received close to 100 pumpkins and gourds this year.
“Our animals love pumpkins and they’re also great for them. They are great for their gut health and great for their skin,” Beaumont said.
Beaumont Acres is home to nearly 30 rescue and retired working animals, including horses, pigs, ducks and a cow.
“Our cow, Trixie, loves pumpkins. She’ll come running across the field for them,” she said.
Trixie the cow is one of the many animals at Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., that enjoys eating pumpkins. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Beaumont said each animal likes a different part of the pumpkin: horses like the seeds, ducks and chickens like the gooey insides, and pigs will eat everything.
“Our pigs also love to play with the pumpkins. They find it very stimulating. They’ll roll them around and play with them like they’re a ball,” Beaumont said. “It’s a lot of fun to watch.”
No paint, no candles allowed
It’s important to assess the condition of pumpkins before deciding where to take them, Smith said, adding that any uncarved pumpkins can be used for homemade meals.

For residents planning to take pumpkins to local animal farms, Smith said it’s important to ensure they are clean and in good condition. Pumpkins should not have any paint, metal, toothpicks, candles, wax or other unsafe-to-eat substances on — or in — them, he said.
Beaumont said it’s fine if pumpkins come to her farm a bit squishy, but she is asking people to refrain from bringing anything with mould.
At Beaumont Acres in London, Ont., Cupcake the pig enjoys a gourd and piece of pumpkin that nearby residents donated to the farm. (Kendra Seguin/CBC)
Better options for mouldy and broken pumpkins include sending them to farms with a digester, Smith said, which breaks down organic materials to produce energy.
Put pumpkins in municipal green bins
It's not just farmers doing the work.

Some municipalities are making it easier for residents who want to give pumpkins a second life. Both Woodstock and Tillsonburg, Ont., are offering to collect pumpkins and redistribute them to people who want them for food or livestock.
Of course, another option is always to put the pumpkins in your green bin.
However, generally, if pumpkins are painted, they must go in the garbage.
— Kendra Seguin

articles.title: Manhunt in western Turkey after eight killed in series of shootings
articles.summary: Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.

blocks.text: A manhunt is under way for a suspect in western Turkey after eight people were killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.

Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect, who fled the scene.
The newspaper Milliyet reports that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker was later found stuck in mud, and that the suspect had abandoned it before fleeing on foot.

In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work."
It added: "We pray to God for mercy on the deceased citizens and offer our condolences and patience to their grieving families and loved ones."

articles.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis
articles.summary:
Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse

Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a…

blocks.text: Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.

At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.

Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.
In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.

“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.

Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.

The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.

The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.

Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.

On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.
Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.

“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.
Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.
“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.

“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.

Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.

Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.
Vice-President Pedro Alliana automatically assumes the presidency to complete the constitutional term until August 2028.

About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

articles.title: Bomb hoaxes: Messages reveal how threat was passed on by air traffic control
articles.summary: BBC Verify has been analysing messages after flights across Europe were targeted by fake bomb threats - the second such incident this week.

blocks.text: More than 20 aircraft across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats. It's the second time this week, which the UK has called a "malicious hoax".
BBC Verify has been analysing the messages sent by an aircraft to find out what happens when a flight receives a bomb hoax - as Thomas Copeland explains.
